title: LE PETIT POUCET
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « LE PETIT POUCET », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: «Le Petit Poucet» is the tale that closes Perrault’s Histoires ou contes du temps passé of 1697: a famine drives a woodcutter and his wife to abandon their seven sons in the forest, and the smallest of them, no bigger than a thumb at birth and taken for a fool because he says nothing, brings them home the first time, and afterwards out of an Ogre’s house alive. Perrault tells it dryly, in the language of a household account — meat bought, money spent, children counted — and he softens nothing that the famine or the Ogre does. The page keeps the 1697 spelling («estoit», «forest», «sçavoir», «&» for «et»), which the glossary and the notes take in hand; the reading voice speaks modern French.

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois un Bucheron & une Bucheronne, qui avaient sept enfans tous Garçons ;
sentences.say: Il était une fois un Bûcheron et une Bûcheronne, qui avaient sept enfants tous Garçons ;
sentences.l: there was one time a Woodcutter and a Woodcutter-woman, who had seven children all Boys;
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a woodcutter and his wife, who had seven children, all of them boys;
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «Bucheronne» is the feminine of «Bucheron» ‘woodcutter’, that is, the woodcutter’s wife; the capitals on both are the 1697 printer’s, who capitalises many common nouns. This witness is not consistent about the old imperfect ending: it prints «estoit» here but the modern «avaient», where the older spelling would be «avoient», in the same sentence.

sentences.t: l’aîné n’avoit que dix ans, & le plus jeune n’en avoit que sept.
sentences.say: l’aîné n’avait que dix ans, et le plus jeune n’en avait que sept.
sentences.l: the eldest had not but ten years, and the youngest had not but seven of them.
sentences.i: the eldest was only ten years old, and the youngest only seven.
sentences.n: «ne … que» is ‘only’, shown in the literal line as ‘not … but’. French says how many years a person has, where English says how old he is. «en» in «n’en avoit que sept» is ‘of them’, standing for «ans» ‘years’.

sentences.t: On s’estonnera que le Bucheron ait eu tant d’enfans en si peu de temps ;
sentences.say: On s’étonnera que le Bûcheron ait eu tant d’enfants en si peu de temps ;
sentences.l: One will be astonished that the Woodcutter has had so many children in so little time;
sentences.i: It will be a wonder that the woodcutter had so many children in so little time;
sentences.n: «on» is the indefinite ‘one, people’: the storyteller answers an objection before the reader makes it. «s’estonnera» is the 1697 spelling of «s’étonnera» ‘will be astonished’, and «ait eu» is the perfect subjunctive that follows such a verb.

sentences.t: mais c’est que sa femme allait viste en besogne, & n’en faisait pas moins que deux à la fois.
sentences.say: mais c’est que sa femme allait vite en besogne, et n’en faisait pas moins que deux à la fois.
sentences.l: but it is that his wife went fast at the work, and made no fewer than two of them at a time.
sentences.i: but the fact is that his wife was quick about the business, and made no fewer than two at a time.
sentences.n: «aller viste en besogne» (modern «vite») is ‘to be quick about the job’, a plain phrase for getting work done fast, turned here to getting children. «c’est que» introduces the explanation, ‘the fact is that’. «n’en faisait pas moins que deux» is ‘made no fewer than two of them’: she bore them two at a time, at the least.

sentences.t: Ils estaient fort pauvres, & leurs sept enfans les incommodaient beaucoup, parce qu’aucun d’eux ne pouvait encore gagner sa vie.
sentences.say: Ils étaient fort pauvres, et leurs sept enfants les incommodaient beaucoup, parce qu’aucun d’eux ne pouvait encore gagner sa vie.
sentences.l: They were very poor, and their seven children inconvenienced them much, because none of them could yet earn his living.
sentences.i: They were very poor, and their seven children were a great burden to them, because not one of them could yet earn his own living.
sentences.n: «fort» before an adjective is ‘very’, the ordinary 1697 word where modern French says «très». «incommoder» is ‘to put out, to be a burden to’; the French is milder than the English, but the sense is plain enough: the children cost more than they bring in.

sentences.t: Ce qui les chagrinait encore, c’est que le plus jeune estait fort delicat, & ne disait mot, prenant pour bestise ce qui estait une marque de la bonté de son esprit :
sentences.say: Ce qui les chagrinait encore, c’est que le plus jeune était fort délicat, et ne disait mot, prenant pour bêtise ce qui était une marque de la bonté de son esprit :
sentences.l: What grieved them still, it is that the youngest was very frail, and said not a word, taking for stupidity what was a mark of the goodness of his mind:
sentences.i: What grieved them further was that the youngest was very frail and said not a word — they took for stupidity what was a sign of the soundness of his mind:
sentences.n: «delicat» here is ‘frail, sickly’, said of the body, not ‘delicate’ in the modern English sense. «ne disait mot», without «pas», is the older negative: ‘said not a word’. The participle «prenant» ‘taking’ belongs to the parents, though the French leaves it hanging; «bestise» (modern «bêtise») is ‘stupidity’, and «la bonté de son esprit» is the soundness of his mind, «esprit» being the wit and not the soul.

sentences.t: il estoit fort petit, & quand il vint au monde, il n’estait gueres plus gros que le pouce, ce qui fit que l’on l’appella le Petit Poucet.
sentences.say: il était fort petit, et quand il vint au monde, il n’était guère plus gros que le pouce, ce qui fit que l’on l’appela le Petit Poucet.
sentences.l: he was very small, and when he came into the world, he was hardly bigger than the thumb, which made that they called him Little Thumb.
sentences.i: he was very small, and when he came into the world he was hardly bigger than a thumb, and that is how he came to be called Little Thumb.
sentences.n: «Poucet» is a diminutive of «pouce» ‘thumb’: the boy was no bigger than a thumb when he was born, which is how he got the name. Lectorium keeps one English name, ‘Little Thumb’, in both layers wherever the French says «le petit Poucet». «venir au monde» is ‘to come into the world’, to be born. «gueres» (modern «guère») with «ne» is ‘hardly’, and «ce qui fit que» is ‘which brought it about that’. The witness is not steady about the name: it prints «le Petit Poucet» with a capital here and once again later, «le petit Poucet» elsewhere, and «Pouçet» with a cedilla several times.

sentences.t: Ce pauvre enfant estoit le souffre-douleurs de la maison, & on lui donnoit toûjours le tort.
sentences.say: Ce pauvre enfant était le souffre-douleurs de la maison, et on lui donnait toujours le tort.
sentences.l: This poor child was the suffer-sorrows of the house, and they always gave him the wrong.
sentences.i: This poor child was the household’s whipping-boy, and the blame was always laid on him.
sentences.n: «souffre-douleurs» is built from «souffrir» ‘to suffer’ and «douleur» ‘pain’: the one on whom everyone’s ill temper falls. «donner le tort à quelqu’un» is ‘to put someone in the wrong’, to lay the blame on him. «on» is the indefinite ‘they’, here the rest of the household, and «toûjours» is the 1697 spelling of «toujours».

sentences.t: Cependant il estoit le plus fin, & le plus avisé de tous ses freres, & s’il parloit peu, il écoutoit beaucoup.
sentences.say: Cependant il était le plus fin, et le plus avisé de tous ses frères, et s’il parlait peu, il écoutait beaucoup.
sentences.l: However he was the most sharp, and the most shrewd of all his brothers, and if he spoke little, he listened much.
sentences.i: Yet he was the sharpest and the shrewdest of all his brothers, and if he spoke little, he listened a great deal.
sentences.n: «fin» of a person is ‘sharp, quick to see’, not ‘fine’; «avisé» is ‘shrewd, with his wits about him’. «s’il parloit peu» uses «si» in the sense ‘if, though’, setting the little speech against the much listening.

sentences.t: Il vint une année très-fâcheuse, & la famine fut si grande que ces pauvres gens resolurent de se deffaire de leurs enfans.
sentences.say: Il vint une année très-fâcheuse, et la famine fut si grande que ces pauvres gens résolurent de se défaire de leurs enfants.
sentences.l: There came a year very grievous, and the famine was so great that these poor people resolved to rid themselves of their children.
sentences.i: There came a very grievous year, and the famine was so great that these poor people resolved to rid themselves of their children.
sentences.n: «il vint une année» is impersonal, ‘there came a year’, with the real subject after the verb. «fâcheuse» is ‘grievous, hard’, stronger in 1697 than the modern ‘annoying’, and «se deffaire de» (modern «se défaire de») is ‘to rid oneself of’. «resolurent» is a passé simple, the narrative past of written French; it has no separate English form, and the tale is told in it throughout.

sentences.t: Un soir que ces enfans estoient couchez, & que le Bucheron estoit auprés du feu avec sa femme, il luy dit, le cœur serré de douleur ?
sentences.say: Un soir que ces enfants étaient couchés, et que le Bûcheron était auprès du feu avec sa femme, il lui dit, le cœur serré de douleur ?
sentences.l: One evening when these children were gone to bed, and when the Woodcutter was beside the fire with his wife, he said to her, the heart gripped with grief:
sentences.i: One evening, when the children had gone to bed and the woodcutter was sitting by the fire with his wife, he said to her, his heart gripped with grief:
sentences.n: «un soir que» is ‘one evening when’, with «que» standing for «où». «couchez» (modern «couchés») is ‘gone to bed’; the witness writes many past participles with «-ez» for «-és». French says «le cœur serré», the heart, where English wants ‘his heart’. The witness prints a question mark after «douleur» where the sense requires a colon introducing what he says; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Tu vois bien que nous ne pouvons plus nourrir nos enfans :
sentences.say: Tu vois bien que nous ne pouvons plus nourrir nos enfants :
sentences.l: You see well that we can no longer feed our children:
sentences.i: You can see that we can no longer feed our children:
sentences.n: «nourrir» is ‘to feed’, to keep fed, rather than ‘to nourish’. «ne … plus» is ‘no longer’. Husband and wife say «tu» to each other throughout; the English is ‘you’ either way.

sentences.t: je ne sçaurois les voir mourir de faim devant mes yeux, & je suis resolu de les mener perdre demain au bois, ce qui sera bien aisé, car tandis qu’ils s’amuseront à fagoter, nous n’avons qu’à nous enfuir sans qu’ils nous voient.
sentences.say: je ne saurais les voir mourir de faim devant mes yeux, et je suis résolu de les mener perdre demain au bois, ce qui sera bien aisé, car tandis qu’ils s’amuseront à fagoter, nous n’avons qu’à nous enfuir sans qu’ils nous voient.
sentences.l: I could not see them die of hunger before my eyes, and I am resolved to lead them off to lose them tomorrow in the wood, which will be very easy, for while they busy themselves at bundling faggots, we have only to flee without their seeing us.
sentences.i: I cannot bear to see them die of hunger before my eyes, and I am resolved to take them off tomorrow and lose them in the wood, which will be easy enough, for while they are busy tying up faggots, we have only to steal away without their seeing us.
sentences.n: «je ne sçaurois» (modern «je ne saurais») is the conditional of «sçavoir» used for ‘I could not, I cannot bring myself to’. «les mener perdre» is ‘to take them to lose them’, two verbs run together as French likes: lead them out and leave them lost. «s’amuser à» is ‘to busy oneself with’, not ‘to have fun’, and «fagoter» is to tie up faggots, bundles of cut wood. «n’avoir qu’à» is ‘to have only to’.

sentences.t: Ah ! s’écria la Bucheronne, pourrois-tu bien toy-même mener perdre tes enfans ?
sentences.say: Ah ! s’écria la Bûcheronne, pourrais-tu bien toi-même mener perdre tes enfants ?
sentences.l: Ah! cried the Woodcutter-woman, could you indeed yourself lead your children off to lose them?
sentences.i: Ah! cried the woodcutter’s wife, could you really take your own children off and lose them?
sentences.n: «s’écrier» is ‘to cry out’. «bien» inside the question is not ‘well’ but a strengthener, ‘really, truly’, and «toy-même» (modern «toi-même») is ‘yourself’, laying the deed at his own door. «pourrois-tu» is the conditional of «pouvoir».

sentences.t: Son mary avoit beau luy representer leur grande pauvreté, elle ne pouvoit y consentir ;
sentences.say: Son mari avait beau lui représenter leur grande pauvreté, elle ne pouvait y consentir ;
sentences.l: Her husband might set their great poverty before her as much as he liked, she could not consent to it;
sentences.i: Her husband urged their great poverty upon her in vain: she could not consent to it;
sentences.n: «avoir beau» with an infinitive means to do a thing in vain, however much one does it: «il avoit beau luy representer» is ‘however much he set before her’. «representer» here is ‘to put before someone, to point out’. «y consentir» is ‘to consent to it’, «y» standing for the whole plan.

sentences.t: elle estoit pauvre, mais elle estoit leur mere.
sentences.say: elle était pauvre, mais elle était leur mère.
sentences.l: she was poor, but she was their mother.
sentences.n: The whole objection in six words, with «estoit» on both sides of it: poverty against motherhood. «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était».

sentences.t: Cependant ayant consideré quelle douleur ce luy seroit de les voir mourir de faim, elle y consentit, & alla se coucher en pleurant.
sentences.say: Cependant ayant considéré quelle douleur ce lui serait de les voir mourir de faim, elle y consentit, et alla se coucher en pleurant.
sentences.l: However having considered what grief it would be to her to see them die of hunger, she consented to it, and went to lie down weeping.
sentences.i: Still, having considered what grief it would be to her to see them die of hunger, she consented, and went to bed in tears.
sentences.n: «ce luy seroit» is ‘it would be to her’, with «luy» where modern French writes «lui». «se coucher» is ‘to go to bed’. «en pleurant» is the gerund, ‘while weeping’, where English is readier with a noun, ‘in tears’.

sentences.t: Le petit Poucet oüit tout ce qu’ils dirent, car ayant entendu de dedans son lit qu’ils parloient d’affaires, il s’estoit levé doucement, & s’estoit glissé sous l’escabelle de son pere pour les écouter sans estre vû.
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet ouït tout ce qu’ils dirent, car ayant entendu de dedans son lit qu’ils parlaient d’affaires, il s’était levé doucement, et s’était glissé sous l’escabelle de son père pour les écouter sans être vu.
sentences.l: Little Thumb heard all that they said, for having heard from inside his bed that they were speaking of business, he had got up quietly, and had slipped under his father’s stool to listen to them without being seen.
sentences.i: Little Thumb heard everything they said, for having caught from his bed that they were talking of serious matters, he had risen quietly and slipped under his father’s stool to listen to them without being seen.
sentences.n: «oüit» is the passé simple of «oüir» (modern «ouïr») ‘to hear’, an old verb already in 1697 and now kept only in set phrases; «entendre», which also means ‘to hear’, does the ordinary work in the next clause. «parler d’affaires» is ‘to talk business’, that is, of serious matters. An «escabelle» is a low backless wooden stool. «sans estre vû» is ‘without being seen’.

sentences.t: Il alla se recoucher & ne dormit point le reste de la nuit, songeant à ce qu’il avoit à faire.
sentences.say: Il alla se recoucher et ne dormit point le reste de la nuit, songeant à ce qu’il avait à faire.
sentences.l: He went to lie down again and slept not at all the rest of the night, thinking of what he had to do.
sentences.i: He went back to bed and did not sleep at all the rest of the night, turning over what he had to do.
sentences.n: «ne … point» is a stronger negative than «ne … pas»: ‘not at all’. «songer à» is ‘to think about, to turn over in one’s mind’, not ‘to dream’ here. «se recoucher» carries the «re-» that English gives as ‘back, again’.

sentences.t: Il se leva de bon matin, & alla au bord d’un ruisseau, où il emplit ses poches de petits cailloux blancs, & ensuite revint à la maison.
sentences.say: Il se leva de bon matin, et alla au bord d’un ruisseau, où il emplit ses poches de petits cailloux blancs, et ensuite revint à la maison.
sentences.l: He got up early in the morning, and went to the edge of a brook, where he filled his pockets with little white pebbles, and then came back to the house.
sentences.n: «de bon matin» is ‘early in the morning’, literally ‘of good morning’. «emplir» is the older, plainer form of «remplir» ‘to fill’. The pebbles are white, which is the whole of the plan: they will show against the ground when he comes back to look for them.

sentences.t: On partit, & le petit Poucet ne découvrit rien de tout ce qu’il sçavoit à ses freres.
sentences.say: On partit, et le petit Poucet ne découvrit rien de tout ce qu’il savait à ses frères.
sentences.l: They set out, and Little Thumb disclosed nothing of all that he knew to his brothers.
sentences.i: They set out, and Little Thumb disclosed nothing of what he knew to his brothers.
sentences.n: «on partit» is the indefinite «on» again, ‘they set out’, taking in the whole family. «découvrir» here is ‘to disclose, to let out’, its older sense of uncovering something hidden. «sçavoit» is the 1697 spelling of «savait» ‘knew’.

sentences.t: Ils allerent dans une forest fort épaisse, où à dix pas de distance on ne se voyoit pas l’un l’autre.
sentences.say: Ils allèrent dans une forêt fort épaisse, où à dix pas de distance on ne se voyait pas l’un l’autre.
sentences.l: They went into a forest very thick, where at ten paces’ distance one did not see one another.
sentences.i: They went into a forest so thick that at ten paces apart they could not see one another.
sentences.n: «forest» is the 1697 spelling of «forêt», with the «s» that modern French replaced by a circumflex. A «pas» is a pace, a stride. «on ne se voyoit pas l’un l’autre» is ‘one did not see one another’, the indefinite «on» standing for whoever was in it.

sentences.t: Le Bucheron se mit à couper du bois & ses enfans à ramasser des broutilles pour faire des fagots.
sentences.say: Le Bûcheron se mit à couper du bois et ses enfants à ramasser des broutilles pour faire des fagots.
sentences.l: The Woodcutter set himself to cutting wood and his children to gathering twigs to make faggots.
sentences.i: The woodcutter set to cutting wood and his children to gathering twigs for faggots.
sentences.n: «se mettre à» is ‘to set about, to begin’, and the verb is not said twice: the one «se mit» serves the children as well. «broutilles» are the small twigs and brushwood left after cutting, and a «fagot» is a bundle of them tied for the fire.

sentences.t: Le pere & la mere les voyant occupez à travailler, s’éloignerent d’eux insensiblement, & puis s’enfuirent tout à coup par un petit sentier détourné.
sentences.say: Le père et la mère les voyant occupés à travailler, s’éloignèrent d’eux insensiblement, et puis s’enfuirent tout à coup par un petit sentier détourné.
sentences.l: The father and the mother, seeing them busy at working, drew away from them imperceptibly, and then fled all at once by a little out-of-the-way path.
sentences.i: The father and mother, seeing them busy at work, drew off from them little by little, and then all at once fled by a little side path.
sentences.n: «insensiblement» is ‘imperceptibly, so little at a time that it is not noticed’, not ‘insensitively’. «s’éloigner» is ‘to move away’, built on «loin» ‘far’. «détourné» of a path is ‘turning aside, out of the way’.

sentences.t: Lorsque ces enfans se virent seuls, il se mirent à crier & à pleurer de toute leur force.
sentences.say: Lorsque ces enfants se virent seuls, il se mirent à crier et à pleurer de toute leur force.
sentences.l: When these children saw themselves alone, they set themselves to crying out and weeping with all their strength.
sentences.i: When the children found themselves alone, they fell to crying out and weeping with all their might.
sentences.n: «se virent seuls» is ‘saw themselves alone’, where English says ‘found themselves’. «crier» is ‘to shout, to cry out’, not to weep, which is «pleurer» beside it. «de toute leur force» is ‘with all their strength’, singular in French. The witness prints «il se mirent», with a singular «il» where the plural verb requires «ils»; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Le petit Pouçet les laissoit crier, sçachant bien par où il reviendroit à la maison ;
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet les laissait crier, sachant bien par où il reviendrait à la maison ;
sentences.l: Little Thumb let them cry, knowing well by where he would come back to the house;
sentences.i: Little Thumb let them cry, knowing quite well by what way he would come back home;
sentences.n: «sçachant» is the gerund of «sçavoir» (modern «savoir») ‘to know’, and «par où» is ‘by which way’. The witness spells the name «Pouçet», with a cedilla, here and several times later, beside «Poucet»; it is one name, and Lectorium prints each as it stands.

sentences.t: car en marchant il avoit laissé tomber le long du chemin les petits cailloux blancs qu’il avait dans ses poches.
sentences.say: car en marchant il avait laissé tomber le long du chemin les petits cailloux blancs qu’il avait dans ses poches.
sentences.l: for while walking he had let fall along the way the little white pebbles that he had in his pockets.
sentences.i: for as he walked he had let fall along the way the little white pebbles he had in his pockets.
sentences.n: «en marchant» is the gerund, ‘while walking’. «laisser tomber» is ‘to let fall, to drop’, two verbs side by side as in «mener perdre» above. «le long du chemin» is ‘along the way’.

sentences.t: Il leur dit donc, ne craignez point mes freres, mon Pere & ma Mere nous ont laissez icy, mais je vous rameneray bien au logis, suivez-moy seulement :
sentences.say: Il leur dit donc, ne craignez point mes frères, mon Père et ma Mère nous ont laissez ici, mais je vous ramènerai bien au logis, suivez-moi seulement :
sentences.l: He said to them therefore, fear not at all, my brothers, my Father and my Mother have left us here, but I shall indeed bring you back to the lodging, only follow me:
sentences.i: So he said to them: Do not be afraid, my brothers; my father and mother have left us here, but I shall surely bring you home again — only follow me:
sentences.n: «ne craignez point» is the imperative with the strong negative, ‘do not be afraid at all’. «le logis» is the dwelling, the house one lives in. «bien» after «rameneray» is the strengthener again, ‘surely, well enough’, and «laissez» is the participle «laissés». He says «vous» to his brothers because they are many; the English is ‘you’ throughout.

sentences.t: ils le suivirent, & il les mena jusqu’à leur maison, par le même chemin qu’ils estoient venus dans la forest.
sentences.say: ils le suivirent, et il les mena jusqu’à leur maison, par le même chemin qu’ils étaient venus dans la forêt.
sentences.l: they followed him, and he led them as far as their house, by the same way that they had come into the forest.
sentences.n: «suivirent» and «mena» are passé simples, the narrative past. «par le même chemin qu’ils estoient venus» leaves out the preposition modern French would repeat: ‘by the same way [by which] they had come’. «venir» takes «estre» in the compound past, so «ils estoient venus» is ‘they had come’, not ‘they were come’.

sentences.t: Ils n’oserent d’abord entrer, mais ils se mirent tous contre la porte pour écouter ce que disaient leur pere & leur mere.
sentences.say: Ils n’osèrent d’abord entrer, mais ils se mirent tous contre la porte pour écouter ce que disaient leur père et leur mère.
sentences.l: They dared not at first go in, but they set themselves all against the door to listen to what their father and their mother were saying.
sentences.i: At first they did not dare go in, but they all set themselves against the door to listen to what their father and mother were saying.
sentences.n: «oser» takes no «pas» in older French: «ils n’oserent» is simply ‘they did not dare’. «écouter» is ‘to listen to’, an act of attention, as against «entendre» ‘to hear’. «disaient» is printed here with the modern imperfect ending, where the witness elsewhere prints «-oient».

sentences.t: Dans le moment que le Bucheron & la Bucheronne arriverent chez eux, le seigneur du Vilage leur envoya dix écus qu’il leur devoit il y avoit longtems, & dont ils n’esperoient plus rien :
sentences.say: Dans le moment que le Bûcheron et la Bûcheronne arrivèrent chez eux, le seigneur du Village leur envoya dix écus qu’il leur devait il y avait longtemps, et dont ils n’espéraient plus rien :
sentences.l: At the moment when the Woodcutter and the Woodcutter-woman arrived at their home, the lord of the Village sent them ten écus that he owed them a long time since, and of which they hoped nothing any more:
sentences.i: The very moment the woodcutter and his wife got home, the lord of the village sent them ten écus he had owed them this long while, and which they had given up hoping for:
sentences.n: An «écu» was a silver coin of some weight; ten of them are a windfall to a household that cannot feed its children. «il leur devoit il y avoit longtems» is ‘he had owed them for a long time’, the impersonal «il y a» measuring the time; «longtems» is spelt «longtemps» a few lines later. «il y a» is literally ‘it there has’: the impersonal «il» ‘it’, the adverbial «y» ‘there’ and «avoir» ‘to have’; with a stretch of time, and usually a «que» after it, it is the French for ‘it is … since’. «dont» carries ‘of which’ in one word. «Vilage» is printed with a single l.

sentences.t: Cela leur redonna la vie, car les pauvres gens mouroient de faim.
sentences.say: Cela leur redonna la vie, car les pauvres gens mouraient de faim.
sentences.l: That gave them back life, for the poor people were dying of hunger.
sentences.i: That gave them back their lives, for the poor creatures were dying of hunger.
sentences.n: «redonner» is ‘to give back’, with the «re-» of return. «mourir de faim» is ‘to die of hunger’ and is meant plainly here, not as the English ‘starving’ said of an appetite. «gens» is ‘people’, and is always plural.

sentences.t: Le Bucheron envoya sur l’heure sa femme à la Boucherie.
sentences.say: Le Bûcheron envoya sur l’heure sa femme à la Boucherie.
sentences.l: The Woodcutter sent on the hour his wife to the Butcher’s.
sentences.i: The woodcutter sent his wife to the butcher’s that very hour.
sentences.n: «sur l’heure» is ‘at once, that very hour’. «la Boucherie» is the butcher’s shop; the capital is the 1697 printer’s.

sentences.t: Comme il y avoit longtemps qu’elle n’avoit mangé, elle acheta trois fois plus de viande qu’il n’en falloit pour le soupé de deux personnes.
sentences.say: Comme il y avait longtemps qu’elle n’avait mangé, elle acheta trois fois plus de viande qu’il n’en fallait pour le soupé de deux personnes.
sentences.l: As there was a long time that she had not eaten, she bought three times more meat than there was need of for the supper of two persons.
sentences.i: As it was long since she had eaten, she bought three times more meat than was needed for the supper of two people.
sentences.n: «il y avoit longtemps qu’elle n’avoit mangé» is ‘it was long since she had eaten’, the French putting the length of time first. The «ne» in «qu’il n’en falloit» adds no negation: French slips it in after a comparison and English leaves it out. «soupé» (modern «souper») is the evening meal.

sentences.t: Lorsqu’ils furent rassasiez, la Bucheronne dit, helas, où sont maintenant ces pauvres enfans, ils feroient bonne chere de ce qui nous reste là.
sentences.say: Lorsqu’ils furent rassasiés, la Bûcheronne dit, hélas, où sont maintenant ces pauvres enfants, ils feraient bonne chère de ce qui nous reste là.
sentences.l: When they were filled, the Woodcutter-woman said, alas, where are now these poor children, they would make good cheer of what is left to us there.
sentences.i: When they had eaten their fill, the woodcutter’s wife said: alas, where are those poor children now, they would feast well on what we have left there.
sentences.n: «rassasiez» (modern «rassasiés») is ‘satisfied, full’, said of hunger. «faire bonne chere» is ‘to eat well, to feast’: «chere» was first the face, then the welcome, then the fare set before a guest, and the phrase has nothing to do with «cher» ‘dear’. The witness never accents «helas» (modern «hélas»).

sentences.t: Mais aussi, Guillaume, c’est toy qui les as voulu perdre, j’avois bien dit que nous nous en repentirions, que font-ils maintenant dans cette Forest ?
sentences.say: Mais aussi, Guillaume, c’est toi qui les as voulu perdre, j’avais bien dit que nous nous en repentirions, que font-ils maintenant dans cette Forêt ?
sentences.l: But also, Guillaume, it is you who have wanted to lose them, I had indeed said that we would repent of it, what are they doing now in that Forest?
sentences.i: And besides, Guillaume, it was you who wanted to lose them; I did say we should repent of it — what are they doing now in that forest?
sentences.n: «mais aussi» opens a reproach, ‘and besides, after all’. The woodcutter is given his name only here. «c’est toy qui» throws the blame forward, ‘it is you who’, and «les as voulu perdre» puts the pronoun before «voulu» in the 1697 order, where modern French says «as voulu les perdre». «se repentir de» is ‘to repent of’, with «en» standing for the thing repented.

sentences.t: Helas ! mon Dieu les loups les ont peut-être déjà mangez ;
sentences.say: Hélas ! mon Dieu les loups les ont peut-être déjà mangez ;
sentences.l: Alas! my God, the wolves have perhaps already eaten them;
sentences.n: «mon Dieu» is an ordinary exclamation of dismay rather than an oath or a prayer. «mangez» is the participle «mangés» in the 1697 spelling. The wolves are named here for the first time, and they will be named again at the Ogre’s door.

sentences.t: tu es bien inhumain d’avoir perdu ainsi tes enfans.
sentences.say: tu es bien inhumain d’avoir perdu ainsi tes enfants.
sentences.l: you are indeed inhuman to have lost thus your children.
sentences.i: you are truly unfeeling, to have lost your children so.
sentences.n: «inhumain» is ‘without human feeling, unfeeling’, the reproach made to someone who has put pity aside. «bien» strengthens again, ‘truly’. She says «tu» to her husband all through the quarrel; the English keeps ‘you’.

sentences.t: Le Bucheron s’impatienta à la fin, car elle redit plus de vingt fois qu’ils s’en repentiroient & qu’elle l’avoit bien dit.
sentences.say: Le Bûcheron s’impatienta à la fin, car elle redit plus de vingt fois qu’ils s’en repentiraient et qu’elle l’avait bien dit.
sentences.l: The Woodcutter grew impatient at the end, for she said again more than twenty times that they would repent of it and that she had indeed said it.
sentences.i: The woodcutter lost patience at last, for she said over more than twenty times that they would repent of it and that she had said so.
sentences.n: «s’impatienter» is ‘to lose patience’ and «à la fin» is ‘in the end, at last’. «redire» is ‘to say again’, with the «re-» of repetition; «plus de vingt fois» is not a count but a way of saying ‘over and over’.

sentences.t: Il la menaça de la battre si elle ne se taisoit.
sentences.say: Il la menaça de la battre si elle ne se taisait.
sentences.l: He threatened her to beat her if she did not keep quiet.
sentences.i: He threatened to beat her if she did not hold her tongue.
sentences.n: «menacer quelqu’un de faire» is ‘to threaten someone with doing’, and the literal line keeps that shape. «se taire» is ‘to fall silent, to hold one’s tongue’, which English has no single verb for. «si elle ne se taisoit» stands without the second half of the negative, as older French often leaves it out after «si».

sentences.t: Ce n’est pas que le Bucheron ne fust peut-estre encore plus fâché que sa femme ;
sentences.say: Ce n’est pas que le Bûcheron ne fût peut-être encore plus fâché que sa femme ;
sentences.l: It is not that the Woodcutter was not perhaps still more grieved than his wife;
sentences.i: Not that the woodcutter was not perhaps even more grieved than his wife;
sentences.n: «ce n’est pas que» with the subjunctive «fust» (modern «fût») heads off a wrong conclusion: the storyteller steps forward to say that the man’s temper was not hardness of heart. The «ne» in «ne fust» carries no negation of its own; the sense is that he may well have been the more grieved of the two. «fâché» here is ‘distressed, grieved’, stronger than the modern ‘annoyed’.

sentences.t: mais c’est qu’elle luy rompoit la teste, & qu’il estoit de l’humeur de beaucoup d’autres gens, qui ayment fort les femmes qui disent bien, mais qui trouvent très importunes celles qui ont toûjours bien dit.
sentences.say: mais c’est qu’elle lui rompait la tête, et qu’il était de l’humeur de beaucoup d’autres gens, qui aiment fort les femmes qui disent bien, mais qui trouvent très importunes celles qui ont toujours bien dit.
sentences.l: but it is that she was breaking his head, and that he was of the humour of many other people, who love much the women who say well, but who find very tiresome those who have always said well.
sentences.i: but the fact is that she was wearing him out with her talk, and that he was of the temper of a good many other people, who are very fond of women who speak sense, but find those who have always said so beforehand not to be borne.
sentences.n: «rompre la teste à quelqu’un» is ‘to break someone’s head’, that is, to wear him out with talk. The point turns on a change of tense: «les femmes qui disent bien» are those who speak sense at the time, «celles qui ont toûjours bien dit» those who have always said so already — who never stop saying they told you so. «importunes» is ‘tiresome, not to be borne’, and «ayment» is the 1697 spelling of «aiment».

sentences.t: La Bucheronne estoit tout en pleurs ?
sentences.say: La Bûcheronne était tout en pleurs ?
sentences.l: The Woodcutter-woman was all in tears:
sentences.n: «tout en pleurs» is ‘all in tears’, «tout» here meaning ‘wholly’ rather than a counted ‘all’. The witness prints a question mark where the sense wants a colon before what she says, as it did after «le cœur serré de douleur»; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Helas ! où sont maintenant mes enfans, mes pauvres enfans ?
sentences.say: Hélas ! où sont maintenant mes enfants, mes pauvres enfants ?
sentences.l: Alas! where are now my children, my poor children?
sentences.i: Alas! where are my children now, my poor children?
sentences.n: The same cry as before, with «mes» where she said «ces»: she has stopped speaking of them at a distance.

sentences.t: Elle le dit une fois si haut que les enfans qui étoient à la porte l’ayant entendu se mirent à crier tous ensemble, nous voyla, nous voyla.
sentences.say: Elle le dit une fois si haut que les enfants qui étaient à la porte l’ayant entendu se mirent à crier tous ensemble, nous voilà, nous voilà.
sentences.l: She said it once so loud that the children who were at the door, having heard it, set themselves to crying out all together, here we are, here we are.
sentences.i: She said it once so loud that the children at the door, hearing it, all began to cry out together: here we are, here we are.
sentences.n: «voyla» is a 1697 spelling of «voilà», and «nous voylà» is ‘here we are’ — «voilà» is built from «voi(s)» ‘see’ and «là» ‘there’, so it points: ‘see there’. «l’ayant entendu» is ‘having heard it’, the «l’» standing for what she said. The witness prints «étoient» here and «estoient» elsewhere: the same word, with «é» standing for the older «es».

sentences.t: Elle courut viste leur ouvrir la porte, & leur dit en les embrassant, que je suis aise de vous revoir, mes chers enfans, vous estes bien las, & vous avez bien faim ;
sentences.say: Elle courut vite leur ouvrir la porte, et leur dit en les embrassant, que je suis aise de vous revoir, mes chers enfants, vous êtes bien las, et vous avez bien faim ;
sentences.l: She ran quickly to open the door to them, and said to them while embracing them, how glad I am to see you again, my dear children, you are very weary, and you are very hungry;
sentences.i: She ran quickly to open the door to them, and said to them as she took them in her arms: how glad I am to see you again, my dear children! You are very weary, and very hungry;
sentences.n: «que je suis aise» is an exclamation in which «que» is ‘how’: ‘how glad I am’; «aise» as an adjective is ‘glad, pleased’. «embrasser», built on «bras» ‘arm’, is ‘to take in one’s arms’ rather than ‘to kiss’. «las» is ‘weary’, and «avoir faim» is ‘to have hunger’ where English has ‘to be hungry’. She turns from the «tu» she used to her husband to «vous» for the children, who are many.

sentences.t: & toy, Pierrot, comme te voyla crotté, viens que je te débarboüille.
sentences.say: et toi, Pierrot, comme te voilà crotté, viens que je te débarbouille.
sentences.l: and you, Pierrot, how here you are all muddied, come that I wash your face.
sentences.i: and you, Pierrot, look how muddy you are — come here and let me wash your face.
sentences.n: «comme te voyla crotté» is ‘how muddied you are there’, «voilà» pointing at him. «crotté» is ‘covered in mud’, from «crotte» ‘mud, dirt’, and it returns when the brothers fall in the mire. «débarboüiller» is to wash a face clean, built on «barboüiller» ‘to smear, to daub’. She says «toy», the singular ‘you’, to the one child.

sentences.t: Ce Pierrot estoit son fils aîné, qu’elle aimoit plus que tous les autres, parce qu’il estoit un peu rousseau, & qu’elle estoit un peu rousse.
sentences.say: Ce Pierrot était son fils aîné, qu’elle aimait plus que tous les autres, parce qu’il était un peu rousseau, et qu’elle était un peu rousse.
sentences.l: This Pierrot was her eldest son, whom she loved more than all the others, because he was a little red-haired, and because she was a little red-haired.
sentences.i: This Pierrot was her eldest son, whom she loved more than all the rest, because he was a little red-headed, and she a little red-headed herself.
sentences.n: «rousseau» and «rousse» are the masculine and feminine of the same thing, red or reddish hair; French has two forms and the joke lives in the pair. «Pierrot» is a familiar form of «Pierre». The mother’s reason for loving him best is set down without comment, which is the storyteller’s manner throughout.

sentences.t: Ils se mirent à Table, & mangerent d’un apetit qui faisoit plaisir au Pere & à la Mere, à qui ils racontoient la peur qu’ils avoient euë dans la Forest, en parlant presque toûjours tous ensemble :
sentences.say: Ils se mirent à Table, et mangèrent d’un appétit qui faisait plaisir au Père et à la Mère, à qui ils racontaient la peur qu’ils avaient eue dans la Forêt, en parlant presque toujours tous ensemble :
sentences.l: They set themselves at Table, and ate with an appetite that gave pleasure to the Father and to the Mother, to whom they told the fright that they had had in the Forest, speaking almost always all together:
sentences.i: They sat down to table and ate with an appetite that was a pleasure to their father and mother, to whom they told the fright they had had in the forest, all talking almost always at once:
sentences.n: «manger d’un apetit» is ‘to eat with an appetite’, the «de» marking the manner; «apetit» is printed with one p. «euë» (modern «eue») is the feminine participle of «avoir», agreeing with «la peur». «en parlant … tous ensemble» is the gerund, ‘all speaking together’: seven boys at once.

sentences.t: Ces bonnes gens étoient ravis de revoir leurs enfans avec eux, & cette joie dura tant que les dix écus durerent ;
sentences.say: Ces bonnes gens étaient ravis de revoir leurs enfants avec eux, et cette joie dura tant que les dix écus durèrent ;
sentences.l: These good people were delighted to see their children again with them, and this joy lasted as long as the ten écus lasted;
sentences.n: «ravis» is ‘delighted, carried away’, the participle of «ravir». The sentence turns on «dura … durerent», the same verb twice, joy measured against money, and the English keeps the repetition. «tant que» is ‘as long as’.

sentences.t: mais lors que l’argent fut dépensé ils retomberent dans leur premier chagrin ;
sentences.say: mais lors que l’argent fut dépensé ils retombèrent dans leur premier chagrin ;
sentences.l: but when the money was spent they fell back into their first sorrow;
sentences.n: «lors que» is printed as two words for the modern «lorsque» ‘when’. «retomber» is ‘to fall back’, and «leur premier chagrin» is ‘their earlier grief’, «premier» meaning the one that came first rather than the greatest.

sentences.t: & résolurent de les perdre encore, & pour ne pas manquer leur coup, de les mener bien plus loin que la premiere fois.
sentences.say: et résolurent de les perdre encore, et pour ne pas manquer leur coup, de les mener bien plus loin que la première fois.
sentences.l: and resolved to lose them again, and, so as not to miss their stroke, to lead them much further than the first time.
sentences.i: and resolved to lose them again, and, so as not to fail this time, to take them much further off than the first.
sentences.n: «manquer son coup» is ‘to miss one’s stroke, to fail in what one attempts’; the coolness of the phrase, used of losing children, is the storyteller’s. The second «de» picks «résolurent» up again after the interruption. The witness accents «résolurent» here and printed «resolurent» without the accent earlier.

sentences.t: Ils ne purent parler de cela si secrettement qu’ils ne fussent entendus par le petit Poucet, qui fit son compte de sortir d’affaire comme il avoit déjà fait ;
sentences.say: Ils ne purent parler de cela si secrètement qu’ils ne fussent entendus par le petit Poucet, qui fit son compte de sortir d’affaire comme il avait déjà fait ;
sentences.l: They could not speak of that so secretly that they were not overheard by Little Thumb, who reckoned on getting out of the business as he had already done;
sentences.i: They could not talk of it so secretly but that Little Thumb overheard them, and he reckoned on getting out of the difficulty as he had done before;
sentences.n: «si … que … ne» is ‘so … that … not’, and English usually turns it round: ‘not so secretly but that he heard them’. «fussent» is the imperfect subjunctive, the elevated narrative form that English has nothing to match. «faire son compte de» is ‘to reckon on doing’, and «sortir d’affaire» is ‘to get out of the scrape’.

sentences.t: mais quoyqu’il se fut levé de bon matin pour aller ramasser des petits cailloux, il ne put en venir à bout, car il trouva la porte de la maison fermée à double tour.
sentences.say: mais quoiqu’il se fut levé de bon matin pour aller ramasser des petits cailloux, il ne put en venir à bout, car il trouva la porte de la maison fermée à double tour.
sentences.l: but although he had got up early in the morning to go and gather little pebbles, he could not come to the end of it, for he found the door of the house shut with a double turn.
sentences.i: but although he had risen early to go and gather little pebbles, he could not manage it, for he found the house door double-locked.
sentences.n: «quoyque» (modern «quoique») is ‘although’ and takes the subjunctive «fut» (for «fût»). «venir à bout de» is ‘to come to the end of, to bring off, to manage’. «fermée à double tour» is ‘shut with a double turn’ of the key: double-locked.

sentences.t: Il ne sçavoit que faire lors que la Bucheronne leur ayant donné à chacun un morceau de pain pour leur déjeuné, il songea qu’il pourroit se servir de son pain au lieu de cailloux, en le jettant par miettes le long des chemins où ils passeroient :
sentences.say: Il ne savait que faire lors que la Bûcheronne leur ayant donné à chacun un morceau de pain pour leur déjeuné, il songea qu’il pourrait se servir de son pain au lieu de cailloux, en le jetant par miettes le long des chemins où ils passeraient :
sentences.l: He did not know what to do when, the Woodcutter-woman having given each of them a piece of bread for their breakfast, he thought that he could make use of his bread instead of pebbles, throwing it by crumbs along the ways where they would pass:
sentences.i: He did not know what to do when, the woodcutter’s wife having given each of them a piece of bread for their breakfast, it came to him that he might use his bread instead of pebbles, scattering it in crumbs along the paths they would take:
sentences.n: «ne sçavoir que faire» is ‘not to know what to do’, with «que» for ‘what’. «déjeuné» (modern «déjeuner») was then the first meal of the day. «se servir de» is ‘to make use of’, and «en le jettant par miettes» is the gerund again, ‘throwing it by crumbs’; «jettant» is the 1697 spelling of «jetant».

sentences.t: il le serra donc dans sa poche.
sentences.l: he put it away therefore in his pocket.
sentences.i: so he stowed it away in his pocket.
sentences.n: «serrer» here is ‘to put away, to stow safely’, its older sense, not ‘to squeeze’. «donc» is ‘therefore, so’, drawing the small action out of the thought before it.

sentences.t: Le Pere & la Mere les menerent dans l’endroit de la Forest le plus épais & le plus obscur, & dés qu’ils y furent ils gagnerent un faux-fuyant & les laisserent là.
sentences.say: Le Père et la Mère les menèrent dans l’endroit de la Forêt le plus épais et le plus obscur, et dès qu’ils y furent ils gagnèrent un faux-fuyant et les laissèrent là.
sentences.l: The Father and the Mother led them into the place of the Forest the thickest and the darkest, and as soon as they were there they gained a by-path and left them there.
sentences.i: The father and mother led them to the thickest and darkest part of the forest, and as soon as they were there they slipped off by a side path and left them.
sentences.n: «l’endroit de la Forest le plus épais» puts the superlative after the noun, ‘the place of the forest the thickest’. A «faux-fuyant» is literally a false way out, a side path taken to get off unseen; the modern sense, an evasion in speech, comes from it. «dés que» (modern «dès que») is ‘as soon as’.

sentences.t: Le Petit Poucet ne s’en chagrina pas beaucoup, parce qu’il croyoit retrouver aisément son chemin par le moyen de son pain qu’il avoit semé partout où il avoit passé ;
sentences.say: Le Petit Poucet ne s’en chagrina pas beaucoup, parce qu’il croyait retrouver aisément son chemin par le moyen de son pain qu’il avait semé partout où il avait passé ;
sentences.l: Little Thumb did not grieve much about it, because he believed he would easily find his way again by means of his bread that he had sown everywhere he had passed;
sentences.i: Little Thumb was not much troubled by it, because he believed he would easily find his way again by means of the bread he had sown everywhere he had passed;
sentences.n: «se chagriner de» is ‘to be troubled about’, with «en» standing for the thing. «semer» is ‘to sow’, the word used of scattering seed over a field. «par le moyen de» is ‘by means of’.

sentences.t: mais il fut bien surpris lorsqu’il ne put en retrouver une seule miette, les Oiseaux étoient venus qui avoient tout mangé.
sentences.say: mais il fut bien surpris lorsqu’il ne put en retrouver une seule miette, les Oiseaux étaient venus qui avaient tout mangé.
sentences.l: but he was very surprised when he could not find again a single crumb of it, the Birds had come who had eaten everything.
sentences.i: but he was greatly surprised when he could not find a single crumb of it again: the birds had come and eaten it all.
sentences.n: «les Oiseaux étoient venus qui avoient tout mangé» puts the relative clause after the verb, ‘the birds had come who had eaten it all’, which English will not bear; the idiomatic line joins the two with ‘and’. The loss is given in one flat clause, with no lament.

sentences.t: Les voylà donc bien affligés, car, plus ils marchoient plus ils s’égaroient, & s’enfonçoient dans la Forest.
sentences.say: Les voilà donc bien affligés, car, plus ils marchaient plus ils s’égaraient, et s’enfonçaient dans la Forêt.
sentences.l: There they are then sorely afflicted, for, the more they walked the more they went astray, and sank deeper into the Forest.
sentences.i: So there they were, sorely afflicted, for the more they walked the more they lost their way and sank deeper into the forest.
sentences.n: «les voylà» is ‘there they are’: the storyteller drops into the present for a moment to put the reader beside them, and the idiomatic line keeps the past the rest of the tale uses. «plus … plus» is ‘the more … the more’. «s’égarer» is ‘to stray, to lose one’s way’, and «s’enfoncer» is ‘to sink into, to go deeper in’.

sentences.t: La nuit vint, & il s’éleva un grand vent qui leur faisoit des peurs épouventables.
sentences.say: La nuit vint, et il s’éleva un grand vent qui leur faisait des peurs épouvantables.
sentences.l: The night came, and there rose a great wind that made them frightful fears.
sentences.i: Night came, and a great wind rose that put a dreadful fear into them.
sentences.n: «il s’éleva un grand vent» is impersonal, ‘there rose a great wind’, with the real subject after the verb. «faire des peurs à quelqu’un» is ‘to give someone frights’, where English says ‘frighten’. «épouventables» is the 1697 spelling of «épouvantables» ‘dreadful’.

sentences.t: Ils croyoient n’entendre de tous côtés que des heurlemens de loups qui venoient à eux pour les manger.
sentences.say: Ils croyaient n’entendre de tous côtés que des hurlements de loups qui venaient à eux pour les manger.
sentences.l: They believed they heard on every side nothing but howlings of wolves that were coming to them to eat them.
sentences.i: They thought they heard on every side nothing but the howling of wolves coming towards them to eat them.
sentences.n: «ne … que» again, ‘nothing but’, here inside the infinitive «n’entendre … que». «heurlemens» is the 1697 spelling of «hurlements» ‘howlings’. «croyoient» leaves the fear where it belongs: they believed it, and the storyteller does not say whether any wolf was there.

sentences.t: Ils n’osoient presque se parler ny tourner la teste.
sentences.say: Ils n’osaient presque se parler ni tourner la tête.
sentences.l: They hardly dared speak to one another nor turn the head.
sentences.i: They hardly dared speak to one another or turn their heads.
sentences.n: «oser» without «pas» again: «ils n’osoient presque» is ‘they hardly dared’. «ny» is the 1697 spelling of «ni» ‘nor’. French says «la teste», the head, where English wants ‘their heads’; «teste» is the older spelling of «tête».

sentences.t: Il survint une grosse pluye qui les perça jusqu’aux os ;
sentences.say: Il survint une grosse pluie qui les perça jusqu’aux os ;
sentences.l: There came on a heavy rain that pierced them to the bones;
sentences.i: A heavy rain came on that soaked them to the bone;
sentences.n: «il survint» is impersonal like «il s’éleva» above, ‘there came on’, used of what arrives unlooked for. «percer jusqu’aux os» is ‘to pierce to the bones’, the same picture as the English ‘to the bone’. «pluye» is the 1697 spelling of «pluie».

sentences.t: ils glissoient à chaque pas & tomboient dans la boüe, d’où ils se relevoient tout crottés, ne sçachant que faire de leurs mains.
sentences.say: ils glissaient à chaque pas et tombaient dans la boue, d’où ils se relevaient tout crottés, ne sachant que faire de leurs mains.
sentences.l: they slipped at each step and fell into the mud, from which they got up again all muddied, not knowing what to do with their hands.
sentences.i: they slipped at every step and fell in the mud, and got up again all covered in mud, not knowing what to do with their hands.
sentences.n: «boüe» is «boue» ‘mud’, printed with a diaeresis to show the two vowels sounded apart. «tout crottés» is ‘all muddied’, the word the mother used of Pierrot at the door. «ne sçachant que faire de leurs mains» is ‘not knowing what to do with their hands’, a phrase of helplessness; what exactly it pictures here — hands too muddy to wipe, or simply children at a loss — the French does not say.

sentences.t: Le petit Pouçet grimpa au haut d’un arbre pour voir s’il ne découvrirait rien ;
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet grimpa au haut d’un arbre pour voir s’il ne découvrirait rien ;
sentences.l: Little Thumb climbed to the top of a tree to see whether he would not discover anything;
sentences.i: Little Thumb climbed to the top of a tree to see whether he could not make anything out;
sentences.n: «au haut de» is ‘to the top of’. «pour voir s’il ne découvrirait rien» keeps the hope in negative shape, ‘whether he would not discover anything’, and «découvrir» here is ‘to catch sight of, to make out’. The verb is printed «découvrirait» with the modern conditional ending, where the witness elsewhere prints «-oit».

sentences.t: ayant tourné la teste de tous costés, il vit une petite lueur comme d’une chandelle, mais qui estoit bien loin par delà la Forest.
sentences.say: ayant tourné la tête de tous côtés, il vit une petite lueur comme d’une chandelle, mais qui était bien loin par delà la Forêt.
sentences.l: having turned the head on all sides, he saw a little gleam as of a candle, but which was very far beyond the Forest.
sentences.i: having turned his head every way, he saw a little gleam, as of a candle, but it was a long way off, beyond the forest.
sentences.n: «costés» is the 1697 spelling of «côtés» ‘sides’. A «lueur» is a faint light, a gleam rather than a flame. «par delà» is ‘beyond, on the far side of’. Everything that follows hangs on this light, and it is seen only from the top of a tree.

sentences.t: Il descendit de l’arbre, & lorsqu’il fut à terre, il ne vit plus rien ;
sentences.say: Il descendit de l’arbre, et lorsqu’il fut à terre, il ne vit plus rien ;
sentences.l: He came down from the tree, and when he was on the ground, he saw nothing more;
sentences.n: «ne … plus rien» is ‘nothing any more’, two negatives working together. «à terre» is ‘on the ground’. From the ground the light is behind the trees, which is why he had to climb for it.

sentences.t: cela le desola.
sentences.say: cela le désola.
sentences.l: that desolated him.
sentences.i: that cast him down.
sentences.n: «desoler» (modern «désoler», printed here without its accent) is ‘to leave desolate, to fill with distress’, much stronger in 1697 than the modern French use of the word.

sentences.t: Cependant, ayant marché quelque temps, avec ses freres du costé qu’il avoit veu la lumiere, il la revit en sortant du Bois.
sentences.say: Cependant, ayant marché quelque temps, avec ses frères du côté qu’il avait vu la lumière, il la revit en sortant du Bois.
sentences.l: However, having walked some time, with his brothers on the side where he had seen the light, he saw it again on coming out of the Wood.
sentences.i: Still, having walked some time with his brothers in the direction where he had seen the light, he saw it again as they came out of the wood.
sentences.n: «du costé que» is ‘in the direction in which’, with «que» doing the work of «où». «veu» is the 1697 spelling of the participle «vu» ‘seen’, and «en sortant» is the gerund, ‘on coming out’. «revit» is «voir» with the «re-» of again.

sentences.t: Ils arriverent enfin à la maison où estoit cette chandelle, non sans bien des frayeurs, car souvent ils la perdoient de veuë, ce qui leur arrivoit toutes les fois qu’ils descendoient dans quelques fonds.
sentences.say: Ils arrivèrent enfin à la maison où était cette chandelle, non sans bien des frayeurs, car souvent ils la perdaient de vue, ce qui leur arrivait toutes les fois qu’ils descendaient dans quelques fonds.
sentences.l: They arrived at last at the house where this candle was, not without many frights, for often they lost it from sight, which happened to them every time that they went down into some hollows.
sentences.i: They came at last to the house where the candle was, not without many frights, for they often lost sight of it, which happened every time they went down into a hollow.
sentences.n: «non sans» is ‘not without’, an understatement that carries a great deal. «perdre de veuë» (modern «vue») is ‘to lose sight of’. «des fonds» are the low places of the ground, hollows and dips; from the bottom of one the light is out of sight again, as it was from the foot of the tree.

sentences.t: Ils heurterent à la porte, & une bonne femme vint leur ouvrir.
sentences.say: Ils heurtèrent à la porte, et une bonne femme vint leur ouvrir.
sentences.l: They knocked at the door, and a good woman came to open to them.
sentences.i: They knocked at the door, and a good woman came to open it to them.
sentences.n: «heurter» is ‘to strike, to knock’, and the same verb returns when the Ogre knocks. «une bonne femme» is simply ‘a good woman’ in 1697, with none of the slighting the modern French phrase has taken on. «vint leur ouvrir» is ‘came to open to them’, French leaving the door unsaid.

sentences.t: Elle leur demanda ce qu’ils vouloient.
sentences.say: Elle leur demanda ce qu’ils voulaient.
sentences.l: She asked them what they wanted.
sentences.n: «demander» is ‘to ask’, not ‘to demand’ — a false friend that runs all through French. «ce que» is ‘what’ in a reported question.

sentences.t: Le petit Pouçet luy dit, qu’ils étoient de pauvres enfans qui s’estoient perdus dans la Forest, & qui demandoient à coucher par charité.
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet lui dit, qu’ils étaient de pauvres enfants qui s’étaient perdus dans la Forêt, et qui demandaient à coucher par charité.
sentences.l: Little Thumb said to her, that they were poor children who had lost themselves in the Forest, and who asked to sleep there out of charity.
sentences.i: Little Thumb told her that they were poor children who had lost themselves in the forest, and who begged a bed for the night out of charity.
sentences.n: «de pauvres enfans» uses «de» and not «des» before a plural adjective that stands first, as French still does. «s’estoient perdus» is ‘had lost themselves’, the same verb «perdre» the parents used of losing them on purpose. «demander à coucher» is ‘to ask for a night’s lodging’, and «par charité» is ‘out of charity’, as a beggar asks.

sentences.t: Cette femme les voyant tous si jolis se mit à pleurer, & leur dit, helas ! mes pauvres enfans, où estes-vous venus ?
sentences.say: Cette femme les voyant tous si jolis se mit à pleurer, et leur dit, hélas ! mes pauvres enfants, où êtes-vous venus ?
sentences.l: This woman, seeing them all so pretty, set herself to weeping, and said to them, alas! my poor children, where have you come?
sentences.i: This woman, seeing them all so pretty, fell to weeping and said to them: alas! my poor children, where have you come to?
sentences.n: «joli» is ‘pretty, good to look at’, said of the boys with no suggestion of softness. «où estes-vous venus» is ‘where have you come’, with «venir» taking «estre» in the compound past; English needs the ‘to’ that the French leaves out. Her tears come before her news.

sentences.t: sçavez-vous bien que c’est icy la maison d’un Ogre qui mange les petits enfans.
sentences.say: savez-vous bien que c’est ici la maison d’un Ogre qui mange les petits enfants.
sentences.l: do you know indeed that this is here the house of an Ogre who eats little children.
sentences.i: do you know that this is the house of an Ogre who eats little children?
sentences.n: «icy» (modern «ici») is ‘here’, and «c’est icy la maison» is ‘this here is the house’. An «Ogre» is a man-eating creature of the tales; the word is rare before this book, which is what carried it into ordinary use, and English took it over unchanged. The witness ends the question with a full stop where the sense requires a question mark; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered, and the English line asks the question.

sentences.t: Helas ! Madame, luy répondit le petit Pouçet, qui trembloit de toute sa force, aussi bien que ses freres, que ferons-nous ?
sentences.say: Hélas ! Madame, lui répondit le petit Poucet, qui tremblait de toute sa force, aussi bien que ses frères, que ferons-nous ?
sentences.l: Alas! Madame, answered her Little Thumb, who was trembling with all his strength, as well as his brothers, what shall we do?
sentences.i: Alas! Madame, Little Thumb answered her, trembling with all his might, and his brothers with him, what shall we do?
sentences.n: «luy» is ‘to her’ here: 1697 writes the pronoun «luy» for both genders where modern French writes «lui». «trembler de toute sa force» is ‘to tremble with all one’s strength’, the phrase used of the children’s crying in the wood. He calls her «Madame», the address of respect, while begging at her door.

sentences.t: Il est bien seur que les Loups de la Forest ne manqueront pas de nous manger cette nuit, si vous ne voulez pas nous retirer chez vous.
sentences.say: Il est bien sûr que les Loups de la Forêt ne manqueront pas de nous manger cette nuit, si vous ne voulez pas nous retirer chez vous.
sentences.l: It is very sure that the Wolves of the Forest will not fail to eat us this night, if you will not take us in at your home.
sentences.i: It is quite certain that the wolves of the forest will not fail to eat us tonight, if you will not take us into your house.
sentences.n: «seur» is the 1697 spelling of «sûr» ‘sure’. «ne pas manquer de faire» is ‘not to fail to do’, a way of saying that a thing is bound to happen. «retirer quelqu’un chez soi» is ‘to take someone into one’s house’, from «retirer» ‘to draw in, to withdraw’.

sentences.t: Et cela étant nous aimons mieux que ce soit Monsieur qui nous mange.
sentences.l: And that being so, we prefer that it be Monsieur who eats us.
sentences.i: And that being so, we would rather it were Monsieur who ate us.
sentences.n: «aimer mieux que» is ‘to prefer that’, and it takes the subjunctive «soit». «Monsieur» is the polite word for the master of the house, and the child uses it of the Ogre who is to eat him; the English keeps the French word, as English does with ‘Madame’. «cela étant» is ‘that being so’.

sentences.t: Peut-estre qu’il aura pitié de nous, si vous voulez bien l’en prier.
sentences.say: Peut-être qu’il aura pitié de nous, si vous voulez bien l’en prier.
sentences.l: Perhaps he will have pity on us, if you are willing to beg him for it.
sentences.i: Perhaps he will take pity on us, if you will be so good as to beg it of him.
sentences.n: «peut-estre que» (modern «peut-être») is ‘perhaps’ with a clause after it. «avoir pitié de» is ‘to have pity on’. «vouloir bien» is ‘to be willing, to be so good as to’, and «l’en prier» is ‘to beg him for it’, «en» standing for the pity.

sentences.t: La femme de l’Ogre qui crut qu’elle pourroit les cacher à son mary jusqu’au lendemain matin, les laissa entrer & les mena se chauffer auprés d’un bon feu, car il y avoit un Mouton tout entier à la broche pour le soupé de l’Ogre.
sentences.say: La femme de l’Ogre qui crut qu’elle pourrait les cacher à son mari jusqu’au lendemain matin, les laissa entrer et les mena se chauffer auprès d’un bon feu, car il y avait un Mouton tout entier à la broche pour le soupé de l’Ogre.
sentences.l: The wife of the Ogre, who believed that she could hide them from her husband until the next morning, let them come in and led them to warm themselves beside a good fire, for there was a whole Sheep on the spit for the Ogre’s supper.
sentences.i: The Ogre’s wife, who thought she could hide them from her husband until the next morning, let them in and took them to warm themselves at a good fire, for a whole sheep was on the spit for the Ogre’s supper.
sentences.n: «cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un» is ‘to hide something from someone’, with «à» where English has ‘from’. «se chauffer» is ‘to warm oneself’. A «broche» is the spit turned before an open fire; the fire that warms the children is roasting the Ogre’s supper, and a whole sheep on it is the measure of his appetite.

sentences.t: Comme ils commençoient à se chauffer ils entendirent heurter trois ou quatre grands coups à la porte, c’estoit l’Ogre qui revenoit.
sentences.say: Comme ils commençaient à se chauffer ils entendirent heurter trois ou quatre grands coups à la porte, c’était l’Ogre qui revenait.
sentences.l: As they were beginning to warm themselves they heard knock three or four great blows at the door, it was the Ogre who was coming back.
sentences.i: As they were beginning to warm themselves, they heard three or four great blows struck at the door: it was the Ogre coming home.
sentences.n: «ils entendirent heurter» is ‘they heard [someone] knock’, French letting one verb govern another with no subject named. «c’estoit l’Ogre qui revenoit» throws the news forward, ‘it was the Ogre who was coming back’, which is how French points at the thing that matters.

sentences.t: Aussi tost sa femme les fit cacher sous le lit & alla ouvrir la porte.
sentences.say: Aussi tôt sa femme les fit cacher sous le lit et alla ouvrir la porte.
sentences.l: At once his wife made them hide under the bed and went to open the door.
sentences.n: «aussi tost» (modern «aussitôt») is ‘at once’, printed here as two words. «faire cacher» is the causative, ‘to make hide’: she does not hide them, she has them hide. The bed is the only furniture the tale gives the room, and it will matter.

sentences.t: L’Ogre demanda d’abord si le soupé estoit prest & si on avoit tiré du vin, & aussi-tost se mit à table.
sentences.say: L’Ogre demanda d’abord si le soupé était prêt et si on avait tiré du vin, et aussitôt se mit à table.
sentences.l: The Ogre asked first whether the supper was ready and whether they had drawn wine, and at once set himself at table.
sentences.i: The Ogre asked first whether supper was ready and whether wine had been drawn, and sat down to table at once.
sentences.n: «tirer du vin» is ‘to draw wine’, from the cask into a jug. «d’abord» is ‘first of all’. The witness prints «aussi-tost» with a hyphen here and «aussi tost» without one a line above; Lectorium prints each as it stands.

sentences.t: Le Mouton estoit encore tout sanglant, mais il ne luy en sembla que meilleur.
sentences.say: Le Mouton était encore tout sanglant, mais il ne lui en sembla que meilleur.
sentences.l: The Sheep was still all bloody, but it seemed to him only the better for it.
sentences.n: «tout sanglant» is ‘all bloody’, the meat still red from the fire. «il ne luy en sembla que meilleur» is ‘it seemed to him only the better for it’: «ne … que» ‘only’ again, with «en» ‘on that account’. The Ogre’s taste is given in one clause and not dwelt on.

sentences.t: Il fleuroit à droite & à gauche, disant qu’il sentoit la chair fraiche.
sentences.say: Il fleurait à droite et à gauche, disant qu’il sentait la chair fraîche.
sentences.l: He sniffed to right and to left, saying that he smelled fresh flesh.
sentences.n: «fleurer» is an old verb for giving off a smell, and, as here, for sniffing at one; it has nothing to do with «fleur» ‘flower’. «sentir» does duty in French for smelling both ways, giving off and taking in. «la chair fraiche» is ‘fresh flesh’, meat not yet cooked — and, as he means it, human. The word is printed «fraiche» here and «fraîche» two sentences later.

sentences.t: Il faut luy dit sa femme, que ce soit ce veau que je viens d’habiller que vous sentez.
sentences.say: Il faut lui dit sa femme, que ce soit ce veau que je viens d’habiller que vous sentez.
sentences.l: It must be, his wife said to him, that it is this calf that I have just dressed that you smell.
sentences.i: It must be the calf I have just dressed that you smell, his wife said to him.
sentences.n: «il faut que» with the subjunctive «soit» is ‘it must be that’, a guess put as a necessity. «habiller» of a beast is the butcher’s word, ‘to dress’ the carcass, the same verb as dressing a person. «je viens d’habiller» is ‘I have just dressed’: «venir de» with an infinitive is the French for ‘to have just’. She says «vous» to her husband and he says «tu» to her; both are ‘you’ in the English.

sentences.t: Je sens la chair fraîche, te dis-je encore une fois, reprit l’Ogre en regardant sa femme de travers, & il y a icy quelque chose que je n’entens pas ;
sentences.say: Je sens la chair fraîche, te dis-je encore une fois, reprit l’Ogre en regardant sa femme de travers, et il y a ici quelque chose que je n’entends pas ;
sentences.l: I smell fresh flesh, I tell you once again, went on the Ogre, looking at his wife askance, and there is here something that I do not understand;
sentences.i: I smell fresh flesh, I tell you again, the Ogre went on, looking askance at his wife, and there is something here I do not understand;
sentences.n: «reprendre» in dialogue is ‘to take up again, to go on’, the storyteller’s word for a second speech. «regarder de travers» is ‘to look askance’, sideways and with suspicion. «entendre» here is ‘to understand’, its older sense, and «je n’entens pas» is printed without the «d» of «entends».

sentences.t: en disant ces mots, il se leva de Table, & alla droit au lit.
sentences.say: en disant ces mots, il se leva de Table, et alla droit au lit.
sentences.l: saying these words, he rose from Table, and went straight to the bed.
sentences.i: with these words he rose from table and went straight to the bed.
sentences.n: «en disant ces mots» is the gerund, ‘in saying these words’, a phrase that carries a speech straight into the act that follows it. «droit» used as an adverb is ‘straight’.

sentences.t: Ah, dit-il voilà, donc comme tu veux me tromper maudite femme, je ne sçais à quoi il tient que je ne te mange aussi, bien t’en prend d’estre une vieille beste.
sentences.say: Ah, dit-il voilà, donc comme tu veux me tromper maudite femme, je ne sais à quoi il tient que je ne te mange aussi, bien t’en prend d’être une vieille bête.
sentences.l: Ah, said he, so that is how you want to deceive me, cursed woman, I do not know what it hangs on that I do not eat you too, it is well for you that you are an old beast.
sentences.i: Ah, said he, so that is how you mean to cheat me, you cursed woman! I do not know what keeps me from eating you too — it is lucky for you that you are an old beast.
sentences.n: «tenir à» in this impersonal turn is ‘to depend on, to hang on’, so «je ne sçais à quoi il tient que je ne te mange» is ‘I do not know what it hangs on that I do not eat you’, that is, what holds me back; the «ne» before «mange» adds no negation, as often after such phrases. «bien t’en prend de» is ‘it turns out well for you that’, ‘lucky for you’ — old meat being tough. The witness prints a comma after «voilà» where the sense wants it after «dit-il»; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Voila du Gibier qui me vient bien à propos pour traiter trois Ogres de mes amis, qui doivent me venir voir ces jours-icy.
sentences.say: Voilà du Gibier qui me vient bien à propos pour traiter trois Ogres de mes amis, qui doivent me venir voir ces jours-ci.
sentences.l: Here is Game that comes to me very much to the purpose to entertain three Ogres of my friends, who are to come and see me these days here.
sentences.i: Here is game that comes just in time for me to entertain three Ogres, friends of mine, who are to come and see me one of these days.
sentences.n: «du Gibier» is ‘game’, the word for wild birds and beasts taken in hunting; the Ogre uses it of seven boys. «à propos» is ‘at the right moment, to the purpose’, and «traiter» is ‘to entertain, to give a meal to’. «trois Ogres de mes amis» is French for ‘three of my friends who are Ogres’, and «ces jours-icy» is ‘these days here’, one of these days.

sentences.t: Il les tira de dessous le lit, l’un aprés l’autre.
sentences.say: Il les tira de dessous le lit, l’un après l’autre.
sentences.l: He drew them out from under the bed, one after the other.
sentences.n: «de dessous» is ‘from under’, two prepositions set together, which French allows as English does. «aprés» is printed with an acute where modern French has a grave, «après». The seven are taken out singly, and the sentence is as short as the act.

sentences.t: Ces pauvres enfans se mirent à genoux en luy demandant pardon, mais ils avoient affaire au plus cruël de tous les Ogres, qui bien loin d’avoir de la pitié, les dévoroit déjà des yeux, & disoit à sa femme que ce seroient là de friands morceaux lorsqu’elle leur auroit fait une bonne sausse.
sentences.say: Ces pauvres enfants se mirent à genoux en lui demandant pardon, mais ils avaient affaire au plus cruel de tous les Ogres, qui bien loin d’avoir de la pitié, les dévorait déjà des yeux, et disait à sa femme que ce seraient là de friands morceaux lorsqu’elle leur aurait fait une bonne sauce.
sentences.l: These poor children set themselves on their knees begging his pardon, but they had to do with the cruellest of all the Ogres, who, far from having any pity, was already devouring them with his eyes, and was saying to his wife that those would be dainty morsels when she had made them a good sauce.
sentences.i: The poor children fell on their knees begging his pardon, but they had to do with the cruellest of all Ogres, who, far from feeling any pity, was already devouring them with his eyes and telling his wife that they would be dainty morsels once she had made them a good sauce.
sentences.n: «avoir affaire à» is ‘to have to do with, to be dealing with’, and «bien loin de» is ‘far from’. «dévorer des yeux» is an ordinary French phrase for looking greedily at something, and it is not only a figure here. «friands morceaux» are ‘dainty morsels’, choice bits, and «sausse» is the 1697 spelling of «sauce»: the threat is made in the language of the kitchen throughout.

sentences.t: Il alla prendre un grand Couteau, & en approchant de ces pauvres enfans, il l’aiguisoit sur une longue pierre qu’il tenoit à sa main gauche.
sentences.say: Il alla prendre un grand Couteau, et en approchant de ces pauvres enfants, il l’aiguisait sur une longue pierre qu’il tenait à sa main gauche.
sentences.l: He went to take a great Knife, and while drawing near to these poor children, he was sharpening it on a long stone that he held in his left hand.
sentences.i: He went and fetched a great knife, and as he came towards the poor children he sharpened it on a long stone he held in his left hand.
sentences.n: «aller prendre» is ‘to go and fetch’, two verbs run together. «en approchant» is the gerund, ‘while drawing near’. The «longue pierre» is a whetstone; he sharpens as he walks, which is why the stone is in his hand and not on a bench.

sentences.t: Il en avoit déjà empoigné un, lorsque sa femme luy dit, que voulez-vous faire à l’heure qu’il est, n’aurés-vous pas assez de temps demain matin ?
sentences.say: Il en avait déjà empoigné un, lorsque sa femme lui dit, que voulez-vous faire à l’heure qu’il est, n’aurez-vous pas assez de temps demain matin ?
sentences.l: He had already seized one of them, when his wife said to him, what do you want to do at the hour that it is, will you not have enough time tomorrow morning?
sentences.i: He had already seized one of them when his wife said to him: what do you mean to do at this hour, will you not have time enough tomorrow morning?
sentences.n: «empoigner» is ‘to seize in the fist’, from «poing» ‘fist’. «à l’heure qu’il est» is ‘at the hour it is’, that is, at this time of night. «n’aurés-vous pas» is «n’aurez-vous pas» ‘will you not have’, in the 1697 spelling with «-és». She argues for delay and not for mercy, which is how she saves them.

sentences.t: Tais-toy, reprit l’Ogre, ils en seront plus mortifiés.
sentences.say: Tais-toi, reprit l’Ogre, ils en seront plus mortifiés.
sentences.l: Hold your tongue, went on the Ogre, they will be the more mortified for it.
sentences.i: Hold your tongue, the Ogre went on, they will be the tenderer for it.
sentences.n: «mortifier» is both ‘to humiliate’ and, of meat, ‘to hang it until it grows tender’; the second seems to be what the Ogre means, though the first is not far off and the French does not settle it, which is why the two English lines differ here. «en» is ‘for it, on that account’, and «tais-toy» is the imperative of «se taire», ‘hold your tongue’.

sentences.t: Mais vous avez encore là tant de viande, reprit sa femme :
sentences.l: But you have still there so much meat, went on his wife:
sentences.i: But you have so much meat there still, his wife went on:
sentences.n: «tant de» is ‘so much, so many’, and «là» is ‘there’, pointing at what is already in the house. She does not plead for the children; she counts the larder, which is the only argument he will hear.

sentences.t: voilà un Veau, deux & la moitié d’un cochon.
sentences.say: voilà un Veau, deux et la moitié d’un cochon.
sentences.l: here is a Calf, two, and the half of a pig.
sentences.i: here is a calf, two, and half a pig.
sentences.n: «voilà» points again, ‘here is’. «deux» stands with nothing to count: the noun that should follow it is missing from the witness, and nothing in the text says what it was, though a sheep is on the spit and a calf has just been dressed. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered, and the English leaves the gap where the French leaves it.

sentences.t: Tu as raison, dit l’Ogre, donne-leur bien à souper affin qu’ils ne maigrissent pas, & va les mener coucher.
sentences.say: Tu as raison, dit l’Ogre, donne-leur bien à souper afin qu’ils ne maigrissent pas, et va les mener coucher.
sentences.l: You are right, said the Ogre, give them well to sup so that they do not grow thin, and go and lead them to bed.
sentences.i: You are right, said the Ogre, give them a good supper so that they do not grow thin, and go and put them to bed.
sentences.n: «avoir raison» is ‘to be right’, literally ‘to have reason’, and «donner à souper» is ‘to give supper to’. «affin que» (modern «afin que») is ‘so that’ and takes the subjunctive «maigrissent», from «maigrir» ‘to grow thin’, built on «maigre» ‘lean’. He is fattening them, and says so.

sentences.t: La bonne femme fut ravie de joye, & leur porta bien à souper ;
sentences.say: La bonne femme fut ravie de joie, et leur porta bien à souper ;
sentences.l: The good woman was delighted with joy, and brought them plenty to sup on;
sentences.i: The good woman was overjoyed, and brought them plenty for supper;
