sentences.n: «ravie de joye» is ‘carried away with joy’, the same «ravi» used of the parents at their own table; «joye» is the 1697 spelling of «joie». In «porter bien à souper» the «bien» is quantity, not manner: plenty to sup on.

sentences.t: mais ils ne purent manger tant ils estoient saisis de peur.
sentences.say: mais ils ne purent manger tant ils étaient saisis de peur.
sentences.l: but they could not eat, so much were they seized with fear.
sentences.i: but they could not eat, so seized were they with fear.
sentences.n: «tant» heading a clause is ‘so much so that’, giving the cause after the fact. «saisi de peur» is ‘seized with fear’, the fear taking hold like a hand.

sentences.t: Pour l’Ogre, il se remit à boire ravis d’avoir de quoy si bien regaler ses Amis.
sentences.say: Pour l’Ogre, il se remit à boire ravis d’avoir de quoi si bien régaler ses Amis.
sentences.l: As for the Ogre, he set himself to drinking again, delighted to have the wherewithal to regale his Friends so well.
sentences.i: As for the Ogre, he fell to drinking again, delighted to have the means of entertaining his friends so well.
sentences.n: «pour» at the head of a sentence is ‘as for’, and «se remettre à» is ‘to set about again’. «de quoy» (modern «de quoi») is ‘the wherewithal, what is needed’, and «regaler» is ‘to entertain with good food’. The witness prints the plural «ravis» where the singular «ravi» is wanted, the Ogre alone being delighted; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Il but une douzaine de coups de plus qu’à l’ordinaire, ce qui luy donna un peu dans la teste, & l’obligea de s’aller coucher.
sentences.say: Il but une douzaine de coups de plus qu’à l’ordinaire, ce qui lui donna un peu dans la tête, et l’obligea de s’aller coucher.
sentences.l: He drank a dozen draughts more than usual, which went a little to his head, and obliged him to go to bed.
sentences.n: A «coup» of drink is a draught, a swallow, not a cup. «à l’ordinaire» is ‘as usual’, and «donner un peu dans la teste» is ‘to go a little to the head’, as English says it too. «s’aller coucher» sets the pronoun before both verbs in the 1697 order, where modern French says «aller se coucher».

sentences.t: L’Ogre avoit sept filles qui n’étoient encore que des enfans.
sentences.say: L’Ogre avait sept filles qui n’étaient encore que des enfants.
sentences.l: The Ogre had seven daughters who were not yet anything but children.
sentences.i: The Ogre had seven daughters, who were still only children.
sentences.n: «ne … que» is ‘not … but’, that is ‘only’; with «encore» ‘yet, still’ it says they were as yet nothing more than children. «avoit» and «étoient» are the imperfect, modern «avait» and «étaient»: 1697 writes this tense in -oit, and it runs through every page of the book. «enfans» is the spelling of «enfants» ‘children’.

sentences.t: Ces petites Ogresses avoient toutes le teint fort beau, parce qu’elles mangeoient de la chair fraîche comme leur pere ;
sentences.say: Ces petites Ogresses avaient toutes le teint fort beau, parce qu’elles mangeaient de la chair fraîche comme leur père ;
sentences.l: These little Ogresses had all of them the complexion very fine, because they ate fresh flesh like their father.
sentences.i: These little Ogresses all had very fine complexions, because they ate fresh flesh, as their father did.
sentences.n: «le teint» is the colour and quality of the skin of the face, ‘complexion’. «fort» before an adjective is the ordinary 1697 intensifier, ‘very’, and it is used again and again in this tale. «chair» is flesh, the meat of a body, and the sentence means it as it sounds. «pere» is printed without the accent of «père».

sentences.t: mais elles avoient de petits yeux gris & tout ronds, le nez crochu & une fort grande bouche avec de longues dents fort aiguës & fort éloignées l’une de l’autre.
sentences.say: mais elles avaient de petits yeux gris et tout ronds, le nez crochu et une fort grande bouche avec de longues dents fort aiguës et fort éloignées l’une de l’autre.
sentences.l: but they had little grey eyes and quite round, the nose hooked and a very big mouth with long teeth very sharp and very far one from the other.
sentences.i: but they had small grey eyes, quite round, hooked noses, and very large mouths with long teeth, very sharp and set wide apart.
sentences.n: French puts most adjectives after the noun, so «yeux gris & tout ronds» is ‘grey and quite round eyes’; the literal line keeps the French order. «le nez crochu» and «une fort grande bouche» are singular where English says ‘noses’ and ‘mouths’, since each of the seven has one. «&» is the printer’s sign for «et» ‘and’, and the book uses it everywhere.

sentences.t: Elles n’estoient pas encore fort méchantes ;
sentences.say: Elles n’étaient pas encore fort méchantes ;
sentences.l: They were not yet very wicked.
sentences.n: «estoient» is another spelling of the same imperfect ‘they were’, modern «étaient»; the book prints «étoient» and «estoient» within a few lines of each other. «méchant» is ‘wicked, given to harm’, a stronger word here than the modern ‘naughty’.

sentences.t: mais elles promettoient beaucoup, car elles mordoient déjà les petits enfans pour en succer le sang.
sentences.say: mais elles promettaient beaucoup, car elles mordaient déjà les petits enfants pour en sucer le sang.
sentences.l: but they promised much, for they already bit the little children to suck the blood of them.
sentences.i: but they gave great promise, for they were already biting little children to suck their blood.
sentences.n: «promettre» ‘to promise’ is used as it is of a young plant or a young talent: they showed every sign of what they would become. «en» in «pour en succer le sang» is ‘of them’, where English says ‘their’. «succer» is the spelling of «sucer» ‘to suck’.

sentences.t: On les avoit fait coucher de bonne heure, & elles estoient toutes sept dans un grand lit, ayant chacune une Couronne d’or sur la teste.
sentences.say: On les avait fait coucher de bonne heure, et elles étaient toutes sept dans un grand lit, ayant chacune une Couronne d’or sur la tête.
sentences.l: One had made them lie down early, and they were all seven in a big bed, having each one a Crown of gold on the head.
sentences.i: They had been put to bed early, and all seven were in one big bed, each with a gold crown on her head.
sentences.n: «on» is the impersonal ‘one’, and French uses it where English prefers the passive: «on les avoit fait coucher» ‘they had been put to bed’. «faire» with an infinitive is ‘to have something done’. «de bonne heure» is ‘early’, literally ‘at a good hour’, and «teste» is the 1697 spelling of «tête» ‘head’. The capitals on «Couronne» are the printer’s.

sentences.t: Il y avoit dans la même chambre un autre lit de la même grandeur ce fut dans ce lit que la femme de l’Ogre mit coucher les sept petits garçons, aprés quoi elle s’alla coucher auprés de son mary.
sentences.say: Il y avait dans la même chambre un autre lit de la même grandeur ce fut dans ce lit que la femme de l’Ogre mit coucher les sept petits garçons, après quoi elle s’alla coucher auprès de son mari.
sentences.l: There was in the same room another bed of the same size; it was in this bed that the wife of the Ogre put to bed the seven little boys, after which she went to lie down beside her husband.
sentences.i: In the same room there was another bed of the same size; it was in this bed that the Ogre’s wife put the seven little boys, after which she went to bed beside her husband.
sentences.n: «il y avoit» is the French for ‘there was’, made of «il» ‘it’, «y» ‘there’ and «avoit» ‘had’. The witness prints nothing at all between «grandeur» and «ce fut»; the sense requires a stop there, and the English supplies one, but Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «elle s’alla coucher» sets the pronoun before the verb, the usual 1697 order where modern French says «elle alla se coucher». «mary» is «mari» ‘husband’, and «aprés» is «après» ‘after’.

sentences.t: Le petit Pouçet qui avoit remarqué que les filles de l’Ogre avoient des Couronnes d’or sur la teste, & qui craignoit qu’il ne prit à l’Ogre quelques remords de ne les avoir pas égorgés dés le soir même, se leva vers le milieu de la nuit,
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet qui avait remarqué que les filles de l’Ogre avaient des Couronnes d’or sur la tête, et qui craignait qu’il ne prit à l’Ogre quelques remords de ne les avoir pas égorgés dès le soir même, se leva vers le milieu de la nuit,
sentences.l: Little Thumb, who had noticed that the daughters of the Ogre had Crowns of gold on the head, and who feared that there might take the Ogre some remorse at not having cut their throats from that very evening, rose towards the middle of the night,
sentences.i: Little Thumb, who had noticed that the Ogre’s daughters had gold crowns on their heads, and who feared the Ogre might be seized with some remorse at not having cut their [the boys’] throats that very evening, got up about the middle of the night,
sentences.n: «Poucet» is a diminutive of «pouce» ‘thumb’: the boy was no bigger than a thumb when he was born, which is how he got the name. Lectorium keeps one English name, ‘Little Thumb’, in both layers wherever the French says «le petit Poucet». The book prints the name «Poucet» and «Pouçet» by turns. In «qu’il ne prit à l’Ogre quelques remords», «il» is impersonal and «quelques remords» is the real subject: ‘that some remorse should take the Ogre’; the «ne» after a verb of fearing adds no negation. «les» in «de ne les avoir pas égorgés» is the boys, not the Ogre’s daughters, who are named in the clause before; the idiomatic line supplies that in brackets. «se leva» is the passé simple, the narrative past tense of written French, used for a single completed act; it carries the whole story, while the imperfect «avoit», «craignoit» gives what was going on around it. «dés» is «dès» ‘from, as early as’.

sentences.t: & prenant les bonnets de ses freres & le sien, il alla tout doucement les mettre sur la teste des sept filles de l’Ogre, aprés leur avoir osté leurs Couronnes d’or, qu’il mit sur la teste de ses freres & sur la sienne, affin que l’Ogre les prit pour ses filles, & ses filles pour les garçons qu’il vouloit égorger.
sentences.say: et prenant les bonnets de ses frères et le sien, il alla tout doucement les mettre sur la tête des sept filles de l’Ogre, après leur avoir ôté leurs Couronnes d’or, qu’il mit sur la tête de ses frères et sur la sienne, afin que l’Ogre les prit pour ses filles, et ses filles pour les garçons qu’il voulait égorger.
sentences.l: and taking the caps of his brothers and his own, he went quite softly to put them on the head of the seven daughters of the Ogre, after having taken off from them their Crowns of gold, which he put on the head of his brothers and on his own, so that the Ogre should take them for his daughters, and his daughters for the boys whose throats he wanted to cut.
sentences.i: and taking his brothers’ caps and his own, he went very softly and set them on the heads of the Ogre’s seven daughters, having first taken their gold crowns off them, which he put on his brothers’ heads and on his own, so that the Ogre should take them for his daughters, and his daughters for the boys whose throats he meant to cut.
sentences.n: «bonnet» is the soft cap worn in bed. «osté» is the spelling of «ôté», from «ôter» ‘to take off’, and «affin que» is «afin que» ‘so that’, which takes the subjunctive: «prit» stands for «prît», the imperfect subjunctive, which 1697 often prints without its circumflex. That tense is the elevated subjunctive of written French and the tale reaches for it after every verb of wishing, fearing and purpose. «égorger», built on «gorge» ‘throat’, is ‘to cut the throat of’, and the English keeps the throat in it wherever the word comes.

sentences.t: La chose réüssit comme il l’avoit pensé :
sentences.say: La chose réussit comme il l’avait pensé :
sentences.l: The thing succeeded as he had thought it.
sentences.i: It fell out just as he had thought.
sentences.n: «la chose» is ‘the thing’, here the whole scheme. «réüssit» is «réussit» ‘succeeded’, printed with a diaeresis to show that the u is sounded apart from the e. French keeps the object pronoun «l’» ‘it’, set before the auxiliary in «il l’avoit pensé», where English drops it.

sentences.t: car l’Ogre s’étant éveillé sur le minuit, eut regret d’avoir differé au lendemain ce qu’il pouvoit executer la veille, il se jetta donc brusquement hors du lit,
sentences.say: car l’Ogre s’étant éveillé sur le minuit, eut regret d’avoir différé au lendemain ce qu’il pouvait exécuter la veille, il se jeta donc brusquement hors du lit,
sentences.l: for the Ogre, having woken about midnight, had regret at having put off to the morrow what he could carry out the evening before; he threw himself therefore abruptly out of the bed,
sentences.i: for the Ogre, waking about midnight, was sorry to have put off till the morrow what he might have done the evening before; so he flung himself abruptly out of bed,
sentences.n: «sur le minuit» is ‘about midnight’, and «avoir regret de» is ‘to be sorry to’. «la veille» is the day or evening before the one spoken of, as «le lendemain» is the day after: from the Ogre’s midnight, the murder he postponed belongs to «la veille». «differé» and «executer» are printed without the accents modern French gives «différé» and «exécuter», and «jetta» doubles the t where modern French writes «jeta».

sentences.t: & prenant son grand Couteau, allons voir, dit il, comment se portent nos petits drolles, n’en faisons pas à deux fois ;
sentences.say: et prenant son grand Couteau, allons voir, dit il, comment se portent nos petits drôles, n’en faisons pas à deux fois ;
sentences.l: and taking his big Knife, let us go and see, said he, how our little rascals are doing, let us not do it at two goes.
sentences.i: and taking his great knife, Let us go and see, said he, how our little rascals are faring; let us not set about it twice.
sentences.n: «comment se portent» is ‘how they are doing’, the phrase used of health. «drolle» (modern «drôle») is a familiar word for a young fellow, a rascal, with no fondness in it here. «n’en faisons pas à deux fois» is a set phrase, ‘let us not take two goes at it’: the work is to be finished at one stroke. 1697 printing gives speech no quotation marks, and the witness prints «dit il» without its hyphen.

sentences.t: il monta donc à tâtons à la Chambre de ses filles & s’approcha du lit où étoient les petits garçons, qui dormoient tous excepté le petit Pouçet, qui eut bien peur lorsqu’il sentit la main de l’Ogre qui luy tastoit la teste, comme il avoit tasté celle de tous ses freres.
sentences.say: il monta donc à tâtons à la Chambre de ses filles et s’approcha du lit où étaient les petits garçons, qui dormaient tous excepté le petit Poucet, qui eut bien peur lorsqu’il sentit la main de l’Ogre qui lui tâtait la tête, comme il avait tâté celle de tous ses frères.
sentences.l: he went up therefore gropingly to the Chamber of his daughters and drew near to the bed where were the little boys, who were all sleeping except Little Thumb, who had great fear when he felt the hand of the Ogre which felt him the head, as he had felt that of all his brothers.
sentences.i: so he groped his way up to his daughters’ chamber and came to the bed where the little boys were, all of them asleep except Little Thumb, who was very much afraid when he felt the Ogre’s hand feeling his head, as he had felt those of all his brothers.
sentences.n: «à tâtons» is ‘groping, feeling one’s way in the dark’, and the verb «taster» (modern «tâter») ‘to feel with the hand’ follows in «luy tastoit la teste». «luy» there is the dative, ‘to him’: French says ‘felt him the head’ where English says ‘felt his head’, and it does the same with every part of the body. «avoir peur» is ‘to be afraid’, literally ‘to have fear’. In «comme il avoit tasté» the «il» is the Ogre: it cannot stand for «la main», which is feminine.

sentences.t: L’Ogre, qui sentit les Couronnes d’or ; vrayment, dit-il, j’allois faire là un bel ouvrage, je voy bien que je bus trop hier au soir.
sentences.say: L’Ogre, qui sentit les Couronnes d’or ; vraiment, dit-il, j’allais faire là un bel ouvrage, je vois bien que je bus trop hier au soir.
sentences.l: The Ogre, who felt the Crowns of gold; truly, said he, I was going to do there a fine piece of work, I see well that I drank too much yesterday evening.
sentences.i: The Ogre, who felt the gold crowns — Truly, said he, I was about to do a fine piece of work there; I see well enough that I drank too much last evening.
sentences.n: The sentence has no main verb: «L’Ogre, qui sentit les Couronnes d’or» sets up a subject and then breaks off into his words. The witness prints it so, with a semicolon, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «un bel ouvrage» is said in scorn, much as English says ‘a fine piece of work’. «vrayment» and «je voy» are the spellings of «vraiment» and «je vois» ‘I see’; «je bus» is the passé simple of «boire» ‘to drink’.

sentences.t: Il alla ensuite au lit de ses filles, où ayant senti les petits bonnets des garçons.
sentences.l: He went next to the bed of his daughters, where having felt the little caps of the boys.
sentences.i: He went next to his daughters’ bed, where, having felt the boys’ little caps —
sentences.n: The sentence breaks off again: «où ayant senti les petits bonnets des garçons» has no main verb to follow it, and the witness closes it with a full stop before the Ogre speaks. The sense runs straight on into his next words, and the English leaves the break open as the French does.

sentences.t: Ah, les voilà, dit-il, nos gaillards ? Travaillons hardiment ;
sentences.l: Ah, there they are, said he, our strapping fellows? Let us work boldly.
sentences.i: Ah, here they are, said he, our fine fellows! Let us set to work, and boldly.
sentences.n: «voilà» is ‘there they are’, made of «voir» ‘to see’ in its command form and «là» ‘there’. «gaillard» is a strapping, lively fellow; the Ogre means the boys he believes he has found. The witness ends the first sentence with a question mark where the sense is an exclamation, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «hardiment» is ‘boldly, without flinching’.

sentences.t: en disant ces mots, il coupa sans balancer la gorge à ses sept filles.
sentences.l: in saying these words, he cut without wavering the throat to his seven daughters.
sentences.i: As he said these words, he cut his seven daughters’ throats without hesitating.
sentences.n: «en disant» is the gerund, ‘(while) saying’. «balancer» here is ‘to waver, to hesitate’, the older sense of weighing one thing against another. «couper la gorge à» puts the person in the dative, ‘to cut the throat to someone’, where English says ‘cut someone’s throat’.

sentences.t: Fort content de cette expedition, il alla se recoucher auprés de sa femme.
sentences.say: Fort content de cette expédition, il alla se recoucher auprès de sa femme.
sentences.l: Very pleased with this expedition, he went to lie down again beside his wife.
sentences.i: Well pleased with this piece of business, he went back to bed beside his wife.
sentences.n: «expedition» (modern «expédition») is not a journey here but a piece of business briskly dispatched. «content de» is ‘pleased with’, and «se recoucher» is «coucher» with «re-» ‘again’, ‘to go back to bed’.

sentences.t: Aussi-tost que le petit Poucet entendit ronfler l’Ogre, il reveilla ses freres, & leur dit de s’habiller promptement & de le suivre.
sentences.say: Aussitôt que le petit Poucet entendit ronfler l’Ogre, il réveilla ses frères, et leur dit de s’habiller promptement et de le suivre.
sentences.l: As soon as Little Thumb heard the Ogre snore, he woke his brothers, and told them to dress themselves promptly and to follow him.
sentences.i: As soon as Little Thumb heard the Ogre snoring, he woke his brothers and told them to dress quickly and follow him.
sentences.n: «aussi-tost», printed with its hyphen and its s, is «aussitôt» ‘as soon as’. «entendre» with a bare infinitive is ‘to hear someone do something’: «entendit ronfler l’Ogre» ‘heard the Ogre snore’. «s’habiller» is ‘to dress oneself’; the same verb returns in the Ogre’s order to his wife, where it does not mean what she takes it to mean.

sentences.t: Ils descendirent doucement dans le Jardin, & sauterent par-dessus les murailles.
sentences.say: Ils descendirent doucement dans le Jardin, et sautèrent par-dessus les murailles.
sentences.l: They went down softly into the Garden, and jumped over the walls.
sentences.n: «muraille» is a thick wall of stone, the wall that encloses a place, where «mur» would be any wall. «sauterent» is the passé simple, printed without the accent of «sautèrent». «doucement» is ‘softly, quietly’, from «doux» ‘soft, sweet’.

sentences.t: Ils coururent presque toute la nuit, toûjours en tremblant & sans sçavoir où ils alloient.
sentences.say: Ils coururent presque toute la nuit, toujours en tremblant et sans savoir où ils allaient.
sentences.l: They ran almost all the night, always trembling and without knowing where they were going.
sentences.i: They ran almost the whole night, trembling all the while and with no notion where they were going.
sentences.n: «toûjours», printed with a circumflex, is «toujours»: here ‘all the while’ rather than ‘always’. «en tremblant» is the gerund again, ‘(while) trembling’. «sçavoir» is the 1697 spelling of «savoir» ‘to know’; its ç comes from a mistaken guess at the word’s Latin ancestry and is dropped in the next century.

sentences.t: L’Ogre s’estant éveillé dit à sa femme, vaten la haut habiller ces petits droles d’hier au soir ;
sentences.say: L’Ogre s’étant éveillé dit à sa femme, va-t-en la haut habiller ces petits drôles d’hier au soir ;
sentences.l: The Ogre, having woken, said to his wife, be off up there to dress those little rascals of yesterday evening.
sentences.i: The Ogre, having woken, said to his wife, Be off upstairs and dress those little rascals of last night.
sentences.n: «vaten la haut» is «va-t’en là-haut» ‘be off up there’, printed without its hyphens, its apostrophe and its accent; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «habiller» is ‘to dress’, and that is how his wife takes it, but the word has a butcher’s sense too, ‘to dress a carcass for the pot’, and that is what he means. The English keeps ‘dress’, which carries both. He speaks to her as «tu» throughout, and the English stays ‘you’.

sentences.t: L’Ogresse fut fort estonnée de la bonté de son mary, ne se doutant point de la maniere qu’il entendoit qu’elle les habillast, & croyant qu’il lui ordonnoit de les aller vestir, elle monta en haut, où elle fut bien surprise lorsqu’elle aperçut ses sept filles égorgées & nageant dans leur sang.
sentences.say: L’Ogresse fut fort étonnée de la bonté de son mari, ne se doutant point de la manière qu’il entendait qu’elle les habillât, et croyant qu’il lui ordonnait de les aller vêtir, elle monta en haut, où elle fut bien surprise lorsqu’elle aperçut ses sept filles égorgées et nageant dans leur sang.
sentences.l: The Ogress was very astonished at the goodness of her husband, not suspecting at all the manner in which he meant that she should dress them, and believing that he was ordering her to go and clothe them, she went up above, where she was much surprised when she caught sight of her seven daughters with their throats cut and swimming in their blood.
sentences.i: The Ogress was much astonished at her husband’s kindness, never suspecting in what manner he meant her to dress them, and believing he was ordering her to go and put their clothes on; she went upstairs, where she was greatly surprised to see her seven daughters with their throats cut and swimming in their blood.
sentences.n: «se douter de» is ‘to suspect’, not ‘to doubt’. «entendoit» is ‘meant, intended’, another of that verb’s old senses beside ‘heard’, and «habillast» is the imperfect subjunctive after it. «vestir» (modern «vêtir») ‘to clothe’ is the plain sense she reads into «habiller». «estonnée» is «étonnée», at this date a stronger word than ‘astonished’: struck as by a blow. «les aller vestir» again sets the pronoun before the infinitive.

sentences.t: Elle commença par s’évanoüir (car c’est le premier expedient que trouvent presque toutes les femmes en pareilles rencontres.)
sentences.say: Elle commença par s’évanouir (car c’est le premier expédient que trouvent presque toutes les femmes en pareilles rencontres.)
sentences.l: She began by fainting (for it is the first expedient that almost all women find in like encounters.)
sentences.i: She began by fainting away (for that is the first expedient almost all women hit upon on such occasions).
sentences.n: «commencer par» is ‘to begin by (doing)’. The narrator steps forward here in his own voice and in the present tense, as he does again over the boots; the remark is at the women’s expense and the English gives it as it stands. «rencontre» is the occasion, the situation one meets with, not a meeting. «expedient» is a way out of a difficulty, and «pareil» is ‘like, of that sort’. The witness sets the full stop inside the closing bracket.

sentences.t: L’Ogre craignant que sa femme ne fût trop longtemps à faire la besongne dont il l’avoit chargée, monta en haut pour luy aider.
sentences.say: L’Ogre craignant que sa femme ne fût trop longtemps à faire la besogne dont il l’avait chargée, monta en haut pour lui aider.
sentences.l: The Ogre, fearing that his wife might be too long at doing the work with which he had charged her, went up above to help her.
sentences.i: The Ogre, fearing his wife would be too long about the work he had charged her with, went upstairs to help her.
sentences.n: «estre longtemps à faire» is ‘to be a long time doing’. «besongne» (modern «besogne») is the task, the job of work — his word for what he has left her to do. The «ne» after «craindre que» is once more the one that adds no negation, and «fût» is the imperfect subjunctive of «estre». «luy aider» takes the dative, ‘to help to her’, where modern French says «l’aider».

sentences.t: Il ne fut pas moins estonné que sa femme lorsqu’il vit cet affreux spectacle.
sentences.say: Il ne fut pas moins étonné que sa femme lorsqu’il vit cet affreux spectacle.
sentences.l: He was not less astonished than his wife when he saw this frightful sight.
sentences.i: He was no less astonished than his wife when he saw that frightful sight.
sentences.n: «ne … pas moins que» is ‘no less than’, an understatement of the kind the tale likes. «affreux» is built on the old noun «affre» ‘dread’: what fills one with dread. «spectacle» is anything set before the eyes, a sight.

sentences.t: Ah, qu’ay-je fait là s’écria-t-il, ils me le payeront les malheureux, & tout à l’heure.
sentences.say: Ah, qu’ai-je fait là s’écria-t-il, ils me le payeront les malheureux, et tout à l’heure.
sentences.l: Ah, what have I done there, he cried out, they will pay me for it, the wretches, and right this hour.
sentences.i: Ah, what have I done! he cried; they shall pay me for it, the wretches, and this very hour.
sentences.n: «qu’ay-je fait là» is ‘what have I done there’, with «là» pointing at the deed; the witness gives the exclamation no mark of its own. «ils me le payeront» is ‘they will pay me it’, with «me» the dative and «le» standing for the whole business. «tout à l’heure» meant at this date ‘at once, this very moment’, not ‘in a little while’ as it does now. «les malheureux» is thrown in after the verb, the French way of naming who is meant.

sentences.t: Il jetta aussitost une potée d’eau dans le nez de sa femme,
sentences.say: Il jeta aussitôt une potée d’eau dans le nez de sa femme,
sentences.l: He threw at once a potful of water in the nose of his wife,
sentences.i: He at once threw a potful of water in his wife’s face,
sentences.n: «une potée» is as much as a pot will hold. «dans le nez» is ‘in the nose’: the water goes full in her face, and the idiomatic line says so. «aussitost» is «aussitôt» ‘at once’.

sentences.t: & l’ayant fait revenir, donne-moy viste mes bottes de sept lieuës, luy dit-il, afin que j’aille les attraper.
sentences.say: et l’ayant fait revenir, donne-moi vite mes bottes de sept lieues, lui dit-il, afin que j’aille les attraper.
sentences.l: and having made her come back, give me quickly my boots of seven leagues, said he to her, so that I may go and catch them.
sentences.i: and having brought her round, Give me my seven-league boots quickly, said he to her, that I may go and catch them.
sentences.n: «lieuës» is the 1697 spelling of «lieues» ‘leagues’; a league was a measure of road distance that varied from place to place, roughly two and a half to three miles. The Sleeping Beauty explains the boots in its own words, printing «lieues» without the diaeresis: boots with which one covered seven leagues in a single stride. In Little Thumb they are also «Fées», ‘enchanted’, and fit whoever puts them on. «faire revenir» is ‘to bring round’ from a faint, «revenir» being ‘to come back’. «donne-moy» is the «tu» form he uses to his wife, and «viste» is «vite» ‘quickly’. «afin que» takes the subjunctive «j’aille».

sentences.t: Il se mit en campagne, & aprés avoir couru bien loin de tous costés, enfin il entra dans le chemin où marchoient ces pauvres enfans qui n’étoient plus qu’à cent pas du logis de leur pere.
sentences.say: Il se mit en campagne, et après avoir couru bien loin de tous côtés, enfin il entra dans le chemin où marchaient ces pauvres enfants qui n’étaient plus qu’à cent pas du logis de leur père.
sentences.l: He put himself in the field, and after having run very far on all sides, at last he came into the road where were walking these poor children who were no more but a hundred paces from the dwelling of their father.
sentences.i: He took the field, and after running far and wide on every side, at last he came into the road where these poor children were walking, no more than a hundred paces now from their father’s house.
sentences.n: «se mettre en campagne» is to take the field, as an army does, and so to set out on a hunt. «ne … plus que» is ‘no more than’, the «ne … que» that opened the Ogresses’ description with «plus» added. «costés» is «côtés» ‘sides’, and «logis» is the dwelling, the place one lodges.

sentences.t: Ils virent l’Ogre qui alloit de montagne en montagne, & qui traversoit des rivieres aussi aisément qu’il auroit fait le moindre ruisseau.
sentences.say: Ils virent l’Ogre qui allait de montagne en montagne, et qui traversait des rivières aussi aisément qu’il aurait fait le moindre ruisseau.
sentences.l: They saw the Ogre who went from mountain to mountain, and who crossed rivers as easily as he would have done the least brook.
sentences.i: They saw the Ogre going from mountain to mountain, and crossing rivers as easily as he would have crossed the smallest brook.
sentences.n: French uses a relative clause, «l’Ogre qui alloit», where English prefers a participle, ‘the Ogre going’. «auroit fait» is ‘would have done’, «faire» standing in for the verb already used, as English may say ‘as he would have done’. «rivieres» is printed without the accent of «rivières».

sentences.t: Le petit Poucet qui vit un rocher creux proche le lieu où ils estoient, y fit cacher ses six freres, & s’y fourra aussi, regardant toûjours ce que l’Ogre deviendroit.
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet qui vit un rocher creux proche le lieu où ils étaient, y fit cacher ses six frères, et s’y fourra aussi, regardant toujours ce que l’Ogre deviendrait.
sentences.l: Little Thumb, who saw a hollow rock near the place where they were, made his six brothers hide there, and thrust himself in there too, watching all the while what the Ogre would become.
sentences.i: Little Thumb, who saw a hollow rock near the place where they were, made his six brothers hide in it, and squeezed in himself, watching all the while what would become of the Ogre.
sentences.n: «y» is ‘there, in it’, and it stands before the verb: «y fit cacher» ‘made hide there’. «se fourrer» is to push oneself into a tight place. «ce que l’Ogre deviendroit» is ‘what the Ogre would become’, the French way of asking what would become of him; «deviendroit» is the conditional, the future seen from a point in the past.

sentences.t: L’Ogre qui se trouvoit fort las du long chemin qu’il avoit fait inutilement, (car les bottes de sept lieuës fatiguent fort leur homme), voulut se reposer,
sentences.say: L’Ogre qui se trouvait fort las du long chemin qu’il avait fait inutilement, (car les bottes de sept lieues fatiguent fort leur homme), voulut se reposer,
sentences.l: The Ogre, who found himself very weary of the long road that he had made to no purpose (for the boots of seven leagues tire their man greatly), wanted to rest himself,
sentences.i: The Ogre, who found himself very weary of the long road he had travelled for nothing (for the seven-league boots tire the man who wears them), wished to rest,
sentences.n: «se trouver» with an adjective is ‘to find oneself, to be’, and «las» is ‘weary’. «faire du chemin» is ‘to cover ground’, and «inutilement» is ‘uselessly, for nothing’. «leur homme» is ‘their man’, whoever has them on — the narrator’s second aside, again in the present tense. The boots are the ones the Ogre called for: ‘the boots of seven leagues’ in the literal line, ‘the seven-league boots’ in the idiomatic one.

sentences.t: & par hasard il alla s’asseoir sur la roche où les petits garçons s’estoient cachés.
sentences.say: et par hasard il alla s’asseoir sur la roche où les petits garçons s’étaient cachés.
sentences.l: and by chance he went to sit down on the rock where the little boys had hidden themselves.
sentences.i: and by chance he went and sat down on the very rock where the little boys were hidden.
sentences.n: «par hasard» is ‘by chance’. The tale has just called it «un rocher creux» and now says «la roche»; both are the same stone. «s’estoient cachés» is the pluperfect of a reflexive verb, ‘had hidden themselves’.

sentences.t: Comme il n’en pouvoit plus de fatigue il s’endormit aprés s’estre reposé quelque temps,
sentences.say: Comme il n’en pouvait plus de fatigue il s’endormit après s’être reposé quelque temps,
sentences.l: As he could do no more for weariness, he fell asleep after having rested himself some time,
sentences.i: As he was quite worn out with weariness, he fell asleep after resting a while,
sentences.n: «n’en pouvoir plus» is a set phrase, ‘to be able to do no more, to be worn out’, with «en» standing for whatever has exhausted one. «s’endormir» is ‘to fall asleep’, «dormir» with the reflexive marking the moment of entering sleep. «aprés s’estre reposé» is ‘after having rested oneself’.

sentences.t: & vint à ronfler si effroyablement que les pauvres enfans n’eurent pas moins de peur que quand il tenoit son grand Couteau pour leur couper la gorge.
sentences.say: et vint à ronfler si effroyablement que les pauvres enfants n’eurent pas moins de peur que quand il tenait son grand Couteau pour leur couper la gorge.
sentences.l: and came to snore so frightfully that the poor children had not less fear than when he held his big Knife to cut them the throat.
sentences.i: and fell to snoring so frightfully that the poor children were no less afraid than when he had held his great knife to cut their throats.
sentences.n: «venir à faire» is ‘to fall to doing’, the beginning of something not intended. «si … que» is ‘so … that’. «n’eurent pas moins de peur» is the same understatement as the Ogre’s astonishment a moment ago, and «leur couper la gorge» the same dative: ‘to cut them the throat’.

sentences.t: Le petit Poucet en eut moins de peur, & dit à ses freres de s’enfuir promptement à la maison pendant que l’Ogre dormoit bien fort, & qu’ils ne se missent point en peine de luy.
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet en eut moins de peur, et dit à ses frères de s’enfuir promptement à la maison pendant que l’Ogre dormait bien fort, et qu’ils ne se missent point en peine de lui.
sentences.l: Little Thumb had less fear of it, and told his brothers to flee promptly to the house while the Ogre was sleeping very hard, and that they should not put themselves in any worry about him.
sentences.i: Little Thumb was less frightened by it, and told his brothers to run home quickly while the Ogre was fast asleep, and not to trouble themselves about him.
sentences.n: «en» in «en eut moins de peur» is ‘of it’, of the snoring. «se mettre en peine de» is ‘to trouble oneself about’; «missent» is the imperfect subjunctive of «mettre», brought in by the «que» that stands for the «de» of «dit … de s’enfuir». «dormir bien fort» is ‘to sleep very hard’, that is soundly.

sentences.t: Ils crurent son conseil, & gagnerent viste la maison.
sentences.say: Ils crurent son conseil, et gagnèrent vite la maison.
sentences.l: They believed his advice, and quickly gained the house.
sentences.i: They took his advice, and quickly made their way home.
sentences.n: «croire un conseil» is ‘to trust and act on advice’, where English says ‘take’. «gagner» a place is to reach it, the sense English keeps in ‘to gain the shore’. «viste» is «vite» ‘quickly’.

sentences.t: Le petit Poucet s’estant approché de l’Ogre, lui tira doucement ses bottes, & les mit aussitost ; les bottes estoient fort grandes & fort larges ;
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet s’étant approché de l’Ogre, lui tira doucement ses bottes, et les mit aussitôt ; les bottes étaient fort grandes et fort larges ;
sentences.l: Little Thumb, having come near to the Ogre, gently pulled off from him his boots, and put them on at once; the boots were very big and very wide.
sentences.i: Little Thumb, having come close to the Ogre, gently drew his boots off him and put them on at once; the boots were very large and very wide.
sentences.n: «s’approcher de» is ‘to come near to’. «tirer» is ‘to pull, to draw’, here to draw the boots off, and «lui» is the dative again, ‘from him’. The two «fort» are the 1697 intensifier, ‘very’.

sentences.t: mais comme elles estoient Fées, elles avoient le don de s’agrandir & de s’apetisser selon la jambe de celuy qui les chaussoit, de sorte qu’elles se trouverent aussi justes à ses pieds & à ses jambes que si elles avoient esté faites pour lui.
sentences.say: mais comme elles étaient Fées, elles avaient le don de s’agrandir et de s’apetisser selon la jambe de celui qui les chaussait, de sorte qu’elles se trouvèrent aussi justes à ses pieds et à ses jambes que si elles avaient été faites pour lui.
sentences.l: but as they were fairy, they had the gift of growing bigger and of growing smaller according to the leg of him who put them on, so that they found themselves as exact to his feet and to his legs as if they had been made for him.
sentences.i: but as they were enchanted, they had the gift of growing larger and smaller to suit the leg of whoever put them on, so that they proved as exact a fit for his feet and legs as if they had been made for him.
sentences.n: «Fée» here is an adjective, ‘enchanted, under a fairy’s power’, which is why no scouring will take the blood off the key. Little Thumb uses it of the Ogre’s boots, «comme elles estoient Fées», rendered ‘as they were fairy’ in the literal line and ‘as they were enchanted’ in the idiomatic one. Cinderella’s «Maraine, qui eſtoit Fée» has the same shape but is read as the noun, since the tale goes on to call her «la Fée»: ‘who was a fairy’. «le don» is the gift a fairy bestows, the word used of the fairies’ blessings elsewhere in the book. «chausser» is to put on whatever goes on the foot, and «se trouver» here is ‘to prove to be’. «s’apetisser» (modern «rapetisser») is ‘to grow smaller’, the answer to «s’agrandir».

sentences.t: Il alla droit à la maison de l’Ogre où il trouva sa femme qui pleuroit auprés de ses filles égorgées.
sentences.say: Il alla droit à la maison de l’Ogre où il trouva sa femme qui pleurait auprès de ses filles égorgées.
sentences.l: He went straight to the house of the Ogre where he found his wife who was weeping beside her daughters with their throats cut.
sentences.i: He went straight to the Ogre’s house, where he found his wife weeping beside her daughters with their throats cut.
sentences.n: «égorgées» is the past participle of «égorger» ‘to cut the throat of’, used as an adjective of the daughters. French says «la maison de l’Ogre» where English prefers ‘the Ogre’s house’, and «auprés de» is ‘beside, close by’.

sentences.t: Vostre mary, lui dit le petit Poucet, est en grand danger, car il a esté pris par une troupe de voleurs qui ont juré de le tuër s’il ne leur donne tout son or & tout son argent.
sentences.say: Votre mari, lui dit le petit Poucet, est en grand danger, car il a été pris par une troupe de voleurs qui ont juré de le tuer s’il ne leur donne tout son or et tout son argent.
sentences.l: Your husband, said Little Thumb to her, is in great danger, for he has been taken by a troop of thieves who have sworn to kill him if he does not give them all his gold and all his silver.
sentences.i: Your husband, said Little Thumb to her, is in great danger, for he has been seized by a band of robbers who have sworn to kill him if he does not give them all his gold and all his silver.
sentences.n: «vostre» is «votre», the «vous» form: the boy addresses the Ogress with the distance due to a stranger, where the Ogre says «tu» to her. Both are ‘you’ in the English. «esté» is «été» ‘been’, and «tuër» is «tuer» ‘to kill’, printed with a diaeresis. «argent» is both ‘silver’ and ‘money’; beside «or» ‘gold’ it is the metal. The whole speech is an invention, and the boy tells it in the present and the perfect, as a messenger would.

sentences.t: Dans le moment qu’ils luy tenoient le poignard sur la gorge, il m’a aperceu & m’a prié de vous venir avertir de l’estat où il est, & de vous dire de me donner tout ce qu’il a vaillant sans en rien retenir, parce qu’autrement ils le tuëront sans misericorde :
sentences.say: Dans le moment qu’ils lui tenaient le poignard sur la gorge, il m’a aperçu et m’a prié de vous venir avertir de l’état où il est, et de vous dire de me donner tout ce qu’il a vaillant sans en rien retenir, parce qu’autrement ils le tueront sans miséricorde :
sentences.l: At the moment when they were holding him the dagger on the throat, he has caught sight of me and has begged me to come and warn you of the state he is in, and to tell you to give me all that he has of worth without keeping back anything of it, because otherwise they will kill him without mercy.
sentences.i: At the moment when they were holding a dagger to his throat, he caught sight of me and begged me to come and warn you of the state he is in, and to bid you give me all that he is worth, keeping nothing of it back, for otherwise they will kill him without mercy.
sentences.n: «tout ce qu’il a vaillant» is a set phrase of the time, ‘all that he is worth’, everything he owns. «vous venir avertir» and «sans en rien retenir» put the pronoun before the infinitive, the usual 1697 order where modern French says «venir vous avertir» and «sans rien en retenir». «aperceu» is «aperçu» ‘caught sight of’, and «estat» is «état» ‘state’. «luy … sur la gorge» is the dative once more.

sentences.t: Comme la chose presse beaucoup, il a voulu que je prisse ses bottes de sept lieuës que voilà pour faire diligence, & aussi afin que vous ne croyiez pas que je sois un affronteur.
sentences.say: Comme la chose presse beaucoup, il a voulu que je prisse ses bottes de sept lieues que voilà pour faire diligence, et aussi afin que vous ne croyiez pas que je sois un affronteur.
sentences.l: As the thing presses much, he wanted that I should take his boots of seven leagues that are there in order to make haste, and also so that you should not believe that I am an impostor.
sentences.i: As the matter presses hard, he would have me take his seven-league boots, these here, to make haste, and also so that you should not think me an impostor.
sentences.n: «presser» is ‘to be urgent’. «que voilà» is ‘that are there’, pointing at the boots he has on his feet. «faire diligence» is ‘to make haste’. «un affronteur» is one who imposes on people with a bold lie, a cheat; the word has since fallen out of use. «prisse» and «sois» are subjunctives after «vouloir que» and «afin que».

sentences.t: La bonne femme fort effrayée lui donna aussitost tout ce qu’elle avoit :
sentences.say: La bonne femme fort effrayée lui donna aussitôt tout ce qu’elle avait :
sentences.l: The good woman, very frightened, gave him at once all that she had:
sentences.n: «la bonne femme» is a plain way of naming her, ‘the woman’, with no praise in «bonne». «effrayée» is ‘frightened’, from «effrayer» ‘to frighten’, the verb that gives «effroi» ‘terror’.

sentences.t: car cet Ogre ne laissoit pas d’estre fort bon mari, quoiqu’il mangeast les petits enfans.
sentences.say: car cet Ogre ne laissait pas d’être fort bon mari, quoiqu’il mangeât les petits enfants.
sentences.l: for this Ogre did not fail to be a very good husband, although he ate little children.
sentences.i: for this Ogre was a very good husband for all that, though he ate little children.
sentences.n: «ne pas laisser de faire» is ‘not to fail to do, to do all the same’. «quoique» ‘although’ takes the subjunctive, here the imperfect subjunctive «mangeast» («mangeât»). The witness spells the word «mari» here, where the Ogress’s husband was «mary» a page earlier.

sentences.t: Le petit Poucet estant donc chargé de toutes les richesses de l’Ogre s’en revint au logis de son pere, où il fut receu avec bien de la joye.
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet étant donc chargé de toutes les richesses de l’Ogre s’en revint au logis de son père, où il fut reçu avec bien de la joie.
sentences.l: Little Thumb, being then laden with all the riches of the Ogre, came back away to the dwelling of his father, where he was received with much joy.
sentences.i: Little Thumb, laden then with all the Ogre’s riches, came back to his father’s house, where he was received with great joy.
sentences.n: «chargé de» is ‘laden with’, the same verb as the work the Ogre «avoit chargée» on his wife. «s’en revenir» is ‘to come back away’, the «en» marking the leaving of the place one was in. «receu» is «reçu» ‘received’, «joye» is «joie», and «bien de la joye» is ‘much joy’.

sentences.t: Il y a bien des gens qui ne demeurent pas d’accord de cette derniere circonstance, & qui prétendent que le petit Poucet n’a jamais fait ce vol à l’Ogre ;
sentences.say: Il y a bien des gens qui ne demeurent pas d’accord de cette dernière circonstance, et qui prétendent que le petit Poucet n’a jamais fait ce vol à l’Ogre ;
sentences.l: There are many people who do not remain in agreement about this last circumstance, and who maintain that Little Thumb never made this theft on the Ogre.
sentences.i: There are many people who do not agree about this last circumstance, and who maintain that Little Thumb never robbed the Ogre at all.
sentences.n: «demeurer d’accord de» is ‘to agree about’. «prétendre» is ‘to maintain, to claim’, not ‘to pretend’. «faire un vol à quelqu’un» is ‘to commit a theft on someone’, to rob them. The narrator turns here to what other people say of the story, and puts their telling in the present: «il y a», «prétendent», and «assurent», «disent-ils» below.

sentences.t: qu’à la verité, il n’avoit pas fait conscience de luy prendre ses bottes de sept lieuës, parce qu’il ne s’en servoit que pour courir aprés les petits enfans.
sentences.say: qu’à la vérité, il n’avait pas fait conscience de lui prendre ses bottes de sept lieues, parce qu’il ne s’en servait que pour courir après les petits enfants.
sentences.l: that in truth he had not made conscience of taking from him his boots of seven leagues, because he did not use them but to run after little children.
sentences.i: that in truth he made no scruple of taking his seven-league boots from him, because he [the Ogre] used them for nothing but running after little children.
sentences.n: «faire conscience de» is ‘to make a scruple of, to have qualms about’. «se servir de» is ‘to use’, and «ne … que» is ‘not … but’, that is ‘only’. «luy prendre ses bottes» is the dative again, ‘to take from him his boots’. «verité» is printed without the accent of «vérité». «il ne s’en servoit» is the Ogre and not the boy, and the idiomatic line supplies the name in brackets.

sentences.t: Ces gens-là asseurent le sçavoir de bonne part, & même pour avoir bû & mangé dans la maison du bûcheron.
sentences.say: Ces gens-là assurent le savoir de bonne part, et même pour avoir bu et mangé dans la maison du bûcheron.
sentences.l: Those people there assure that they know it from a good quarter, and even for having drunk and eaten in the house of the woodcutter.
sentences.i: Those people declare they know it on good authority, and indeed from having drunk and eaten in the woodcutter’s own house.
sentences.n: «de bonne part» is ‘from a good quarter, on good authority’. «asseurer» is the older spelling of «assurer», which the very next sentence prints the modern way — one of many places where the book spells a word two ways within a few lines. «pour avoir bû» is ‘for having drunk’, giving the ground of their claim.

sentences.t: Ils assurent que lorsque le petit Poucet eut chaussé les bottes de l’Ogre, il s’en alla à la Cour, où il sçavoit qu’on estoit fort en peine d’une Armée, qui estoit à deux cents lieües de là, & du succés d’une bataille qu’on avoit donnée.
sentences.say: Ils assurent que lorsque le petit Poucet eut chaussé les bottes de l’Ogre, il s’en alla à la Cour, où il savait qu’on était fort en peine d’une Armée, qui était à deux cents lieues de là, et du succès d’une bataille qu’on avait donnée.
sentences.l: They assure that when Little Thumb had put on the Ogre’s boots, he went off to the Court, where he knew that one was much troubled about an Army, which was two hundred leagues from there, and about the outcome of a battle that had been given.
sentences.i: They declare that when Little Thumb had put on the Ogre’s boots, he went off to the Court, where he knew there was great anxiety about an army two hundred leagues away, and about the outcome of a battle that had been fought.
sentences.n: «estre en peine de» is ‘to be anxious about’. «donner une bataille» is the set phrase for fighting one. «le succés» is the outcome, what follows on a thing, and need not be a happy one. «lieües» is printed here with the diaeresis over the u and «lieuës» elsewhere in the tale: the same word.

sentences.t: Il alla, disent-ils, trouver le Roi, & luy dit que, s’il le souhaitoit, il luy rapporteroit des nouvelles de l’Armée avant la fin du jour.
sentences.say: Il alla, disent-ils, trouver le Roi, et lui dit que, s’il le souhaitait, il lui rapporterait des nouvelles de l’Armée avant la fin du jour.
sentences.l: He went, say they, to find the King, and said to him that, if he wished it, he would bring him back news of the Army before the end of the day.
sentences.i: He went, they say, to find the King, and told him that, if he wished it, he would bring him news of the army before the end of the day.
sentences.n: «aller trouver quelqu’un» is ‘to go and see someone’, literally ‘to go to find’. The offer goes into reported speech with the conditional «rapporteroit» for what would happen and the imperfect «souhaitoit» for the condition. «des nouvelles» is plural in French where English says ‘news’.

sentences.t: Le Roi lui promit une grosse somme d’argent s’il en venoit à bout.
sentences.say: Le Roi lui promit une grosse somme d’argent s’il en venait à bout.
sentences.l: The King promised him a big sum of money if he came to the end of it.
sentences.i: The King promised him a large sum of money if he brought it off.
sentences.n: «venir à bout de» is ‘to come to the end of’, that is to carry a thing through; «en» stands for the errand. «argent» here is money, not the metal it was beside «or» a page ago.

sentences.t: Le petit Pouçet rapporta des nouvelles dés le soir même ; & cette premiere course l’ayant fait connoître, il gagnoit tout ce qu’il vouloit :
sentences.say: Le petit Poucet rapporta des nouvelles dès le soir même ; et cette première course l’ayant fait connaître, il gagnait tout ce qu’il voulait :
sentences.l: Little Thumb brought back news as early as that very evening; and this first run having made him known, he earned all that he wanted:
sentences.i: Little Thumb brought back news that very evening; and this first errand having made his name, he earned whatever he wanted:
sentences.n: «dés le soir même» is ‘that very evening, as early as that evening’. «une course» is an errand run, the word used of a messenger’s journey. «connoître» is the spelling of «connaître» ‘to know’. The imperfect «gagnoit» opens what became his regular living.

sentences.t: car le roi le payoit parfaitement bien pour porter ses ordres à l’Armée,
sentences.say: car le roi le payait parfaitement bien pour porter ses ordres à l’Armée,
sentences.l: for the king paid him perfectly well for carrying his orders to the Army,
sentences.n: «parfaitement bien» is ‘perfectly well’, that is handsomely. The witness prints «roi» here without the capital it carries everywhere else in the tale, and «Armée» with one.

sentences.t: & une infinité de Dames luy donnoient tout ce qu’il vouloit pour avoir des nouvelles de leurs Amans, & ce fut là son plus grand gain.
sentences.say: et une infinité de Dames lui donnaient tout ce qu’il voulait pour avoir des nouvelles de leurs Amants, et ce fut là son plus grand gain.
sentences.l: and an infinity of Ladies gave him all that he wanted to have news of their Lovers, and that was there his greatest gain.
sentences.i: and any number of ladies gave him whatever he wanted for news of their lovers, and that was his greatest profit of all.
sentences.n: «une infinité de» is ‘a great number of’, no more literal than English ‘no end of’. «Amant» at this date is the man who loves and courts a woman and has said so; it is not the plain modern sense. «ce fut là» is ‘that was’, with «là» pointing, and the passé simple closing the account.

sentences.t: Il se trouvoit quelques femmes qui le chargeoient de Lettres pour leurs maris, mais elles le payoient si mal, & cela alloit à si peu de chose, qu’il ne daignoit mettre en ligne de conte, ce qu’il gagnoit de ce côté-là.
sentences.say: Il se trouvait quelques femmes qui le chargeaient de Lettres pour leurs maris, mais elles le payaient si mal, et cela allait à si peu de chose, qu’il ne daignait mettre en ligne de conte, ce qu’il gagnait de ce côté-là.
sentences.l: There found themselves some wives who charged him with Letters for their husbands, but they paid him so badly, and that came to so little a thing, that he did not deign to put into the line of account what he earned on that side there.
sentences.i: There were some wives who charged him with letters for their husbands, but they paid him so badly, and it came to so little, that he did not deign to reckon up what he earned on that side.
sentences.n: «il se trouvoit» is the impersonal ‘there were, there were to be found’. «mettre en ligne de conte» is «mettre en ligne de compte» ‘to take into account’; 1697 spells «conte» and «compte» alike. «daigner» is ‘to deign, to think a thing worth doing’. The wives who pay badly for word of their husbands stand against the ladies who pay well for word of their lovers.

sentences.t: Aprés avoir fait pendant quelque temps le métier de courier, & y avoir amassé beaucoup de bien, il revint chez son pere, où il n’est pas possible d’imaginer la joye qu’on eut de le revoir.
sentences.say: Après avoir fait pendant quelque temps le métier de courrier, et y avoir amassé beaucoup de bien, il revint chez son père, où il n’est pas possible d’imaginer la joie qu’on eut de le revoir.
sentences.l: After having plied for some time the trade of courier, and having amassed at it much wealth, he came back to his father’s, where it is not possible to imagine the joy that one had at seeing him again.
sentences.i: After plying the courier’s trade for some time, and amassing much wealth at it, he came back to his father’s house, where it is not possible to imagine the joy they had at seeing him again.
sentences.n: «faire le métier de» is ‘to ply the trade of’; «courier» (modern «courrier») is the messenger who carries dispatches. «y» is ‘at it, in that employment’, and «du bien» is property, wealth. «on» stands here for the family, and the English gives it as ‘they’.

sentences.t: Il mit toute sa famille à son aise.
sentences.l: He put all his family at its ease.
sentences.i: He set his whole family at their ease.
sentences.n: «mettre à son aise» is ‘to put in easy circumstances’, to place beyond want; «son» agrees with «famille», so the ease is the family’s and not his.

sentences.t: Il achepta des Offices de nouvelle création pour son pere & pour ses freres, & par là il les établit tous, & fit parfaitement bien sa Cour en même temps.
sentences.say: Il acheta des Offices de nouvelle création pour son père et pour ses frères, et par là il les établit tous, et fit parfaitement bien sa Cour en même temps.
sentences.l: He bought Offices of new creation for his father and for his brothers, and by that he established them all, and made his Court perfectly well at the same time.
sentences.i: He bought newly created offices for his father and his brothers, and by that means set them all up, and paid his court to perfection at the same time.
sentences.n: An «office» was a post under the Crown that a man bought and then held as property; the King raised money by creating new ones to sell, which is «de nouvelle création». «établir» someone is to settle them in a position and an income. «faire sa cour» is ‘to pay one’s court’, to stand well with those in power, so the purchase obliged the King as much as it provided for the family. «achepta» is «acheta» ‘bought’.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ.
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: «Moralité» is the verse moral that closes the tale; the book prints one after every story, and after some a second. The lines that follow are verse, and the English keeps them line for line without rhyming.

«ne … point» is a stronger ‘not at all’ than «ne … pas». «on» is the impersonal ‘one’, standing for people in general. «bien-faits» is ‘well made’, of the shape of a body, and «bien grands» is ‘well grown, tall’. «un extérieur qui brille» is an outward appearance that catches the eye. The French rhymes «enfans» with «grands» and «brille» with «pille» and «famille» below; the English keeps the lines but not the rhyme.

sentences.t:
Mais si l’un d’eux est foible ou ne dit mot,
On le méprise, on le l’aille, on le pille.
sentences.say:
Mais si l’un d’eux est faible ou ne dit mot,
On le méprise, on le l’aille, on le pille.
sentences.l:
But if one of them is weak or says not a word,
One despises him, one mocks him, one plunders him.
sentences.i:
But if one of them is feeble, or never says a word,
He is despised, he is jeered at, he is robbed.
sentences.n: «foible» is the 1697 spelling of «faible» ‘weak’, and it covers weakness of body and of parts. «ne dit mot» is ‘says not a word’. The witness prints «on le l’aille», which is not French; the rhyme with «pille» and the run of the line require «on le raille» ‘they mock him’, which is the reading the English follows, but Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «piller» is ‘to plunder’, here to take from him whatever is his.

sentences.t:
Quelquefois, cependant, c’est ce petit marmot
Qui fera le bonheur de toute la famille.
sentences.say:
Quelquefois, cependant, c’est ce petit marmot,
Qui fera le bonheur de toute la famille.
sentences.l:
Sometimes, however, it is this little brat
Who will make the happiness of all the family.
sentences.i:
Yet sometimes it is this little brat
Who will bring the whole family its happiness.
sentences.n: «marmot» is a small child, named without ceremony — the word for the least of them. «c’est … qui» singles him out, as English does with ‘it is he who’. «fera le bonheur de» is ‘will make the happiness of’, and the moral ends where the tale ended: the smallest and least regarded of the seven is the one who made them all.
